uni-cse-compiler.title: Compiler Design (B.Tech CSE)
uni-cse-compiler.description: Lexing, top-down and LR parsing, syntax-directed translation, intermediate code, run-time environments and optimisation — a complete B.Tech compiler-design course with GATE-style problems and runnable code.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Introduction & Lexical Analysis
courses.summary: Phases and passes of a compiler, compilers vs interpreters, tokens, lexemes and patterns, input buffering, specifying tokens with regular expressions, recognising them with DFAs, and lexer generators (Lex/Flex).
outcomes: Learners can name each compiler phase and its output
Learners can count tokens in a statement
Learners can write regular definitions for tokens
Learners can explain how a lexer generator builds a DFA with longest-match rules

scenes.text: Divya writes `total = price * qty + 10;` in C.
Before the CPU sees it, the compiler takes it through a pipeline of phases.

steps.title: The pipeline
steps.body:
**Front end (analysis):** lexical analysis (characters → tokens) → syntax analysis (tokens → parse tree) → semantic analysis (type checking, scope) → intermediate code generation.
**Back end (synthesis):** machine-independent optimisation → code generation → machine-dependent optimisation.
**Symbol table** and **error handler** interact with all phases.
A **pass** reads the whole program once; several phases may be grouped in one pass. **Cross-compiler:** runs on one machine, generates code for another. **Bootstrapping:** writing a compiler in its own language.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Trace a statement
steps.body:
`total = price * qty + 10;`
- Lexer: ⟨id,1⟩ ⟨=⟩ ⟨id,2⟩ ⟨*⟩ ⟨id,3⟩ ⟨+⟩ ⟨num,10⟩ ⟨;⟩
- Parser: tree with = at the root, + below, * below +.
- Semantic: qty is int and price is float → insert int-to-float conversion.
- TAC: t1 = inttofloat(qty); t2 = price * t1; t3 = t2 + 10.0; total = t3
- Optimiser / code generator then produce machine instructions.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Compiler vs interpreter
steps.body: Compiler: translates the whole program ahead of time; faster execution; errors reported before running (C, Rust). Interpreter: executes statement by statement; slower; easier debugging (classic BASIC, shell). Hybrid: Java compiles to bytecode, then the JVM interprets/JIT-compiles; CPython compiles to bytecode and interprets it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing type checking in the lexer.
- Treating 'phase' and 'pass' as the same.
- Thinking Python has no compilation step (it compiles to bytecode).

activity.prompt: Put the compiler phases in order

quiz.q: Which phase detects an undeclared variable?
quiz.why: An undeclared variable is a semantic error, found in semantic analysis by scope and type checks. The syntax can be perfectly valid.
Lexical analysis reads characters and produces a stream of tokens for the parser.

quiz.q: A compiler that runs on x86 and produces ARM code is a
quiz.why: A cross-compiler runs on one machine (x86) but generates code for a different target (ARM).
The symbol table stores information about names and is used by most phases, from lexical analysis to code generation.

quiz.q: Missing semicolon is usually found by the
quiz.why: A missing semicolon breaks the grammar, so the parser reports it as a syntax error.

scenes.text: Reading `if(x>=10)`, the lexer must decide: is it 'if' or an identifier 'if…'? Is '>=' one token or two?
Rules: longest match, then keywords before identifiers.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Token:** a category (id, num, relop, keyword if) with an optional attribute (pointer to symbol table, value).
- **Lexeme:** the actual character sequence (count, 3.14, >=).
- **Pattern:** the rule describing lexemes of a token (a regular expression).
Lexer tasks: strip whitespace/comments, track line numbers, enter identifiers into the symbol table, report lexical errors (illegal characters, unterminated strings).
**Input buffering:** two-buffer scheme with sentinels (eof markers) to reduce end-of-buffer tests; pointers lexemeBegin and forward.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Count tokens
steps.body: `printf("i = %d", i);` → printf · ( · "i = %d" · , · i · ) · ; = **7 tokens** (the string literal is one token).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Another count
steps.body: `int max(int a, int b) { return a > b ? a : b; }` → int, max, (, int, a, ,, int, b, ), {, return, a, >, b, ?, a, :, b, ;, } = **20 tokens**. Comments and whitespace produce none.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Splitting a string literal into several tokens.
- Counting `>=` as two tokens.
- Counting comments as tokens.

activity.prompt: Count the tokens in one line of C-like code (identifiers/keywords, integers, string literals, two-character operators ==, !=, <=, >=, &&, ||, and any other single non-space character).
activity.starter:
import re
line = input()
# build a regex with alternatives, longest first, and use re.findall
activity.solution:
import re
line = input()
pat = r'"[^"]*"|[A-Za-z_]\w*|\d+|==|!=|<=|>=|&&|\|\||\S'
print(len(re.findall(pat, line)))
activity.hint: Put the string-literal and multi-character alternatives before the single-character catch-all.

quiz.why: The token is the class (id); the lexeme is the actual text matched, here 'count'.
The tokens are a, =, b, +, 25 and ; which makes 6 tokens.
With a sentinel character at the end of each buffer half, the scanner needs only one test per character, instead of two checks for end of buffer.
The lexer discards comments and whitespace, since the parser doesn't need them.
An unterminated string can't be formed into a valid token, so it is a lexical error found by the scanner.

scenes.text: Token rules are regular expressions; a lexer is the DFA that recognises them all at once.
Lex/Flex builds that DFA automatically.

steps.title: Regular definitions and transition diagrams
steps.body:
Regular definitions: letter → [A-Za-z_]; digit → [0-9]; id → letter (letter | digit)*; number → digit⁺ (. digit⁺)? (E [+−]? digit⁺)?; relop → < | <= | = | <> | > | >=.
Each pattern becomes a transition diagram; the lexer combines them (union NFA → DFA). Keywords are usually recognised as identifiers and then looked up in a reserved-word table.

steps.title: Lex / Flex
steps.body: A Lex file has declarations, **rules** (pattern { action }) and user code. Conflict rules: (1) **longest match** wins; (2) among equal lengths, the **earlier rule** wins. So put keyword rules before the identifier rule. The generated scanner uses a DFA table; `yytext` holds the lexeme, `yylex()` returns the next token.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Longest match
steps.body: Input `<=` with rules for `<` and `<=` → lexer reads `<`, sees `=`, continues → token **LE** (longest). Input `<5` → reads `<`, next char `5` cannot extend → retract one character → token **LT**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Keyword vs identifier
steps.body: Rules: 'if' { return IF; } then [a-z]+ { return ID; }. Input `if` → both match length 2 → earlier rule → **IF**. Input `iffy` → identifier rule matches 4 characters (longest) → **ID**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the identifier rule before keywords in Lex.
- Forgetting to retract the extra lookahead character.
- Writing number patterns that accept '1.' or '.5' unintentionally.

statements.s: Lex prefers the longest matching lexeme.
For equal-length matches Lex picks the later rule.
Keywords are often handled as identifiers plus a table lookup.
Lexers are typically based on finite automata.
Balanced parentheses can be checked by the lexer's DFA.

quiz.why: Tokens are specified with regular expressions, which finite automata can recognise. Context-free grammars are used for the syntax.
In Lex, the variable yytext holds the lexeme that the last rule matched.

quiz.q: Input `>=x`, rules for > and >=: first token
quiz.why: Lex follows the longest-match rule. For input '>=x', the rule for '>=' matches 2 characters, longer than '>' (1), so '>=' is the first token.

quiz.q: To make 'while' a keyword in Lex, its rule should be
quiz.why: When two rules match the same length, Lex picks the earlier one. So the keyword rule for 'while' must come before the general identifier rule.
Lex is a scanner generator: from a specification of patterns it produces a lexical analyser (scanner).

scenes.text: A student's file has 12 mistakes. A good compiler reports many of them in one run, not just the first.
Each phase has its own recovery strategy.

steps.title: Strategies
steps.body:
- **Lexical:** panic mode (delete characters until a valid token), insert/delete/replace/transpose a character.
- **Syntax:** **panic mode** (skip tokens until a synchronising token such as ; or }), **phrase-level** (local correction), **error productions** (grammar rules for common mistakes), **global correction** (minimum edits; theoretical).
- **Semantic:** report type mismatches, undeclared identifiers (often insert into symbol table to avoid cascades).
Goals: report clearly with location, recover quickly, avoid cascades of bogus errors, little overhead on correct programs.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Panic mode
steps.body: `x = (a + * b; y = 2;` → error at `*`; skip tokens until `;` (synchronising), resume parsing at `y = 2;` → one error reported, rest of the file still checked.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Error production
steps.body: Grammar adds `stmt → expr error_missing_semicolon` matching `expr` followed by a newline token in a language where ; is required, so the compiler can say 'missing semicolon' precisely.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting global correction in production compilers (too expensive).
- Thinking the lexer can catch syntax errors like unbalanced parentheses.
- Ignoring cascaded errors caused by one real mistake.

activity.prompt: Match the strategy to its description
pairs: Skip input until a synchronising token
Local fix such as inserting a missing ;
Minimum-edit repair of the whole input

quiz.why: In panic-mode recovery the parser skips to a synchronising token, such as ';' or '}', which marks the end of a statement or block, and then resumes.
Global correction finds the smallest set of changes that makes the program correct, but it is too costly, so it is mostly theoretical.

quiz.q: Illegal character '@' in C source is reported by the
quiz.why: A character like '@' doesn't start any valid C token, so no lexer rule matches and the lexer reports it.
A type mismatch is detected during semantic analysis, so it's a semantic error.
A good error-recovery strategy lets the compiler carry on after an error without producing a flood of false, follow-on messages (cascades), so the programmer sees only the real mistakes.

questions.q: First phase of a compiler
questions.why: Lexical analysis (the scanner) is the first phase. It reads the source characters and groups them into tokens.

questions.q: Tokens are specified by
questions.why: Tokens are described by patterns written as regular expressions. Grammars (CFGs) describe the syntax later.

questions.q: Type checking happens in
questions.why: Type checking is part of semantic analysis, which checks meaning beyond the grammar, such as types, scopes and declarations.

questions.q: Tokens in `while (i < 10) i++;`
questions.why: The tokens are while, (, i, <, 10, ), i, ++ and ;, which makes 9.

questions.q: Lex conflict rule for equal-length matches
questions.why: If two Lex rules match the same length, the one written earlier in the specification wins.

questions.q: Java's javac produces
questions.why: javac compiles Java source to bytecode for the JVM, not directly to machine code.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The lexer cannot detect unbalanced parentheses. Reason (R): Balanced parentheses are not a regular language. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: a lexer can't check that parentheses are balanced. R is true and explains it: balanced parentheses need counting, which is not a regular language, so a finite automaton can't do it. A parser is needed.

questions.q: Tokens in `x = y >= 3.14 ? "yes" : "no";`
questions.why: The tokens are x, =, y, >=, 3.14, ?, "yes", :, "no" and ;, which makes 10. Each string and number counts as one token.

questions.q: Number of passes is reduced by
questions.why: Grouping several phases into a single pass reduces the number of passes over the source or intermediate code.

questions.q: Case: a lexer returns ID for 'int'. Most likely cause
options: identifier rule placed before the keyword rule
questions.why: If 'int' is returned as an identifier, the general identifier pattern is matching first. In Lex a keyword rule must appear before the identifier rule, as equal-length matches go to the earlier rule.

questions.q: Input `a+++b` with longest match (C)
questions.why: With the longest-match (maximal munch) rule, the scanner reads '++' as one token before the next '+'. So a+++b is a ++ + b.

questions.q: A cross-compiler is needed when
questions.why: A cross-compiler is needed when the machine that runs the compiler (host) differs from the machine the code is for (target), as with embedded systems.

questions.q: In the two-buffer scheme each buffer half ends with
questions.why: In the two-buffer scheme, each buffer half ends with a sentinel (eof) character, so the scanner needs only one test per character to detect the end of a buffer.

questions.q: Regular definition for C identifiers
questions.why: A C identifier starts with a letter or underscore, followed by any number of letters, digits or underscores: [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*.

questions.q: Tokens in `/* sum */ s = s + a[i]; // add`
questions.why: The lexer removes the comments, leaving s, =, s, +, a, [, i, ] and ;. That is 9 tokens.

questions.q: Which is NOT a front-end task?
questions.why: Register allocation is a back-end task, as it deals with the target machine. Lexing, parsing and type checking belong to the front end.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Syntax Analysis I — Top-Down Parsing
courses.summary: Role of the parser, eliminating left recursion and left factoring, recursive-descent parsing, FIRST and FOLLOW sets, constructing LL(1) tables, checking LL(1)-ness and table-driven predictive parsing.
outcomes: Learners can remove left recursion and left-factor grammars
Learners can compute FIRST and FOLLOW sets
Learners can build and use an LL(1) parsing table
Learners can decide whether a grammar is LL(1)

lessons.title: Preparing grammars: left recursion and left factoring

story.title: A parser stuck in a loop

scenes.text: A recursive-descent parser for E → E + T calls E, which calls E, which calls E… forever.
Rewriting the grammar removes the loop without changing the language.

steps.title: Transformations
steps.body:
**Immediate left recursion:** A → Aα₁ | … | Aαₘ | β₁ | … | βₙ becomes A → β₁A' | … | βₙA', A' → α₁A' | … | αₘA' | ε.
Indirect left recursion (A ⇒⁺ Aα) is removed by ordering variables and substituting first.
**Left factoring:** A → αβ₁ | αβ₂ becomes A → αA', A' → β₁ | β₂ — so one token of lookahead can choose.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Expression grammar
steps.body:
E → E + T | T; T → T * F | F; F → (E) | id becomes
E → T E'; E' → + T E' | ε; T → F T'; T' → * F T' | ε; F → (E) | id.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Left factoring if-else
steps.body: S → if E then S | if E then S else S | a becomes S → if E then S S' | a; S' → else S | ε. (Still ambiguous — the LL(1) table will have a conflict on else, resolved by preferring S' → else S.)

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Indirect
steps.body: S → Aa | b; A → Sc | d. Substitute S into A: A → Aac | bc | d → A → bcA' | dA', A' → acA' | ε.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the ε alternative of A'.
- Removing left recursion but leaving a common prefix (still not LL(1)).
- Missing indirect left recursion.

activity.prompt: Remove left recursion from A → Aa | b. Fill in: A → ___ A' and A' → ___ A' | ε

quiz.why: A top-down parser can't handle left recursion, since the rule A → Aα makes it call itself forever without consuming input.
A → Ab | c produces a c followed by any number of b's: cb*.
Left factoring pulls out the common prefix of alternatives, so a predictive parser can choose a rule using just one lookahead symbol.

quiz.q: After removing left recursion from E → E + T | T
options: E → T E', E' → + T E' | ε
quiz.why: Removing left recursion from E → E + T | T gives E → T E' and E' → + T E' | ε, which generates the same language without left recursion.
S → Aa and A → Sb are indirectly left-recursive: S ⇒ Aa ⇒ Sba, so S appears at the left end again after two steps.

scenes.text: To choose a production, the parser asks: which tokens can start this? which can follow it?
FIRST and FOLLOW answer those two questions.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
**FIRST(X):** terminals that begin strings derived from X (plus ε if X ⇒* ε). For X → Y₁Y₂…: add FIRST(Y₁) − {ε}; if Y₁ is nullable add FIRST(Y₂) − {ε}, etc.; if all nullable add ε.
**FOLLOW(A):** terminals that can appear immediately after A in some sentential form. $ ∈ FOLLOW(S). For B → αAβ: add FIRST(β) − {ε}; if β ⇒* ε (or β empty) add FOLLOW(B) to FOLLOW(A). FOLLOW never contains ε.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Expression grammar
Solved example 2 · Nullable chain
steps.body:
S → ABC; A → a | ε; B → b | ε; C → c.
- FIRST(S) = {a, b, c} (A and B nullable, C not).
- FOLLOW(A) = FIRST(BC) = {b, c}; FOLLOW(B) = {c}; FOLLOW(C) = FOLLOW(S) = {$}.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting ε in FOLLOW.
- Forgetting to add FOLLOW(B) when the rest of the RHS is nullable.
- Stopping at the first symbol when it is nullable.

activity.prompt: Match the set (expression grammar)

quiz.why: The end marker $ is always in FOLLOW(S) for the start symbol S, as S may be followed by the end of the input.
FOLLOW sets contain terminals and $ but never ε, because ε is not a symbol in the input.

quiz.q: S → AB, A → a | ε, B → b: FIRST(S)
quiz.why: A is nullable, so S can begin with whatever A produces (a) or, if A vanishes, whatever B starts with (b). FIRST(S) = {a, b}.

quiz.q: In S → ABC (A, B nullable), FOLLOW(A) includes
quiz.why: FOLLOW(A) includes FIRST(B) minus ε, and, since B can vanish, FIRST(C) too. Nullable symbols are skipped to find what can follow.
T' → * F T' | ε, so FIRST(T') = {*, ε}.

scenes.text: An LL(1) parser is a table: row = variable on top of the stack, column = next token, entry = which production to use.
If every cell has at most one entry, the grammar is LL(1).

steps.title: Construction and test
steps.body:
For each A → α: for every terminal a ∈ FIRST(α), put A → α in M[A, a]; if ε ∈ FIRST(α), put A → α in M[A, b] for every b ∈ FOLLOW(A) (including $). Empty cells = errors.
Grammar is **LL(1)** iff no cell has two entries, i.e. for each pair A → α | β: FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅, and if β ⇒* ε then FIRST(α) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅. Ambiguous or left-recursive grammars are never LL(1).
Parsing: stack holds $ S; repeat: if top is a terminal, match; if a variable, replace it by the table's RHS (reversed push); accept when stack and input are both $.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Table rows
steps.body:
Expression grammar:
- M[E, id] = M[E, (] = E → T E'
- M[E', +] = E' → + T E'; M[E', )] = M[E', $] = E' → ε
- M[T', *] = T' → * F T'; M[T', +] = M[T', )] = M[T', $] = T' → ε
- M[F, id] = F → id; M[F, (] = F → (E)

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Not LL(1)
steps.body:
S → aSb | ab: FIRST(aSb) ∩ FIRST(ab) = {a} → conflict at M[S, a] → **not LL(1)**. Left-factor: S → aS', S' → Sb | b → FIRST(Sb) = {a}, FIRST(b) = {b} → LL(1).
S → A a | b, A → a | ε: FIRST(Aa) = {a}, FIRST(b) = {b} fine; but A → a and A → ε with FOLLOW(A) = {a} → conflict at M[A, a] → **not LL(1)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing ε-productions under FIRST instead of FOLLOW.
- Forgetting the $ column.
- Claiming a grammar is LL(1) after removing left recursion without checking FIRST/FOLLOW overlaps.

activity.prompt: LL(1) or not?

items.text: E → T E'; E' → + T E' | ε; T → id
S → A a | b ; A → a | ε
S → a A | b B ; A → c ; B → c

quiz.why: An ambiguous grammar is never LL(1), because for some input two rules would apply and the parse table cell would have two entries.
An ε-production A → ε is placed in the table columns for the terminals in FOLLOW(A).
The terminal + is in FOLLOW(T'), so on seeing + the parser uses T' → ε.
LL(1) means scanning Left to right, producing a Leftmost derivation, with 1 symbol of lookahead.
A left-recursive grammar is never LL(1). Its table would have conflicts, and a top-down parser would loop.

scenes.text: Write a function for every non-terminal; each function reads tokens and calls others.
The same structure can evaluate expressions as it parses.

steps.title: Technique
steps.body: Predictive recursive descent: function A() chooses a production by looking at the next token (using FIRST/FOLLOW) and calls the functions for its RHS symbols; match(t) consumes the expected terminal or reports an error. With backtracking it can handle more grammars but may be exponential. Hand-written parsers (GCC's C/C++ front ends, Clang, many JSON parsers) are recursive descent.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Functions for E/T/F
steps.body:
E(): v = T(); while next is '+': consume; v += T(); return v
T(): v = F(); while next is '*': consume; v *= F(); return v
F(): if next is '(': consume; v = E(); match(')'); return v; else return number
The while loops are the iterative form of E' and T' and give left associativity.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Trace
steps.body: Input 2 + 3 * 4: E → T → F = 2; T sees +, returns 2; E consumes +, calls T → F = 3, T sees * → F = 4 → 12; E returns 2 + 12 = **14**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing E() { E(); match('+'); T(); } (left recursion → infinite recursion).
- Forgetting to check for unexpected trailing input.
- Mixing up precedence by calling T and F in the wrong layers.

activity.prompt: Write a recursive-descent evaluator for expressions with integers, +, *, and parentheses (no spaces needed; ignore spaces). Print the value.
activity.starter:
s = input().replace(' ', '')
pos = 0
def peek():
    return s[pos] if pos < len(s) else ''
# write E(), T(), F() and print(E())
activity.hint: One function per precedence level; use while loops instead of left recursion.

quiz.why: Recursive descent has a procedure for each non-terminal and builds the parse from the start symbol downwards, so it's a top-down parser.

quiz.q: Left-recursive rule in recursive descent causes
quiz.why: A left-recursive rule A → Aα makes the procedure A() call itself first, before consuming any token, which causes infinite recursion.

quiz.q: While-loops in E() and T() give
quiz.why: Writing the repetition as a while loop accumulates the result from left to right, which gives left associativity (a − b − c = (a − b) − c).
The evaluator handles the parentheses first: (1 + 2) = 3 and (3 + 4) = 7, so the product is 3 × 7 = 21.
Backtracking parsers may try many alternatives repeatedly, so in the worst case they take exponential time.

questions.q: Top-down parsing builds the tree from
questions.why: A top-down parser starts at the start symbol (the root) and expands down toward the leaves.

questions.q: FOLLOW(S) always contains
questions.why: FOLLOW of the start symbol always contains $, the end-of-input marker.

questions.q: A grammar with left recursion is
questions.why: A grammar with left recursion is not LL(1). Eliminate the left recursion first.

questions.q: A → Ac | Ad | e, after removing left recursion
options: A → eA', A' → cA' | dA' | ε
questions.why: For A → Aα | β the fix is A → βA' and A' → αA' | ε. Here α is c or d and β is e: A → eA', A' → cA' | dA' | ε.

questions.q: FIRST(F) for F → (E) | id
questions.why: A factor F → (E) | id begins with either ( or id, so FIRST(F) = {(, id}.

questions.q: LL(1) table entry for ε-production uses
questions.why: In an LL(1) table, an ε-production is entered under the terminals in FOLLOW of its left-hand side, not FIRST.

questions.q: Assertion (A): S → aSb | ab is not LL(1). Reason (R): Both alternatives begin with a. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: S → aSb | ab isn't LL(1). R is true and explains it: both alternatives start with a, so their FIRST sets overlap and one lookahead symbol can't choose between them.

questions.q: S → AB; A → a | ε; B → b | ε. FOLLOW(A)
questions.why: FOLLOW(A) = FIRST(B) minus ε = {b}, plus FOLLOW(S) = {$}, because B is nullable and can vanish. So {b, $}.

questions.q: S → aABb; A → c | ε; B → d | ε. FIRST(ABb)
questions.why: Both A and B can vanish, so FIRST(ABb) includes FIRST(A) = c, FIRST(B) = d and finally b. So {c, d, b}.

questions.q: Case: a team's hand-written parser hangs on 'x - y - z'. The grammar has E → E - T. Fix
questions.why: E → E − T is left-recursive, so a recursive-descent parser calls E() forever. Rewrite the rule to remove the left recursion (a loop form).

questions.q: S → iEtSS' | a; S' → eS | ε; E → b. M[S', e] contains
questions.why: The terminal e is in FIRST(eS), so S' → eS goes in column e. It is also in FOLLOW(S'), so S' → ε goes there too. That conflict is the dangling-else ambiguity.

questions.q: Number of non-empty entries in row E' of the expression LL(1) table
questions.why: E' → + T E' goes under +, and E' → ε goes under the terminals in FOLLOW(E'), which are ) and $. That's 3 non-empty entries.

questions.q: For S → (S)S | ε, FOLLOW(S)
questions.why: In S → (S)S | ε, S is followed by ) in the first occurrence, and the second S inherits FOLLOW(S), which includes $. So FOLLOW(S) = {), $}.

questions.q: S → Aa | bAc | dc | bda; A → d. Is it LL(1)?
questions.why: The alternatives bAc and bda both start with b, so FIRST sets overlap in {b}. With one lookahead symbol the parser can't choose, so it isn't LL(1).

questions.q: Recursive-descent evaluation of 2*3+4*5
questions.why: With precedence, multiplication goes first: 2 × 3 = 6 and 4 × 5 = 20, then 6 + 20 = 26.

questions.q: Grammar S → aSa | bSb | c is
questions.why: The alternatives start with a, b and c respectively, so FIRST sets are disjoint. It has no left recursion, so it is LL(1).

courses.title: Unit 3 · Syntax Analysis II — Bottom-Up (LR) Parsing
courses.summary: Shift-reduce parsing, handles and conflicts, LR(0) items and automaton, SLR(1), canonical LR(1) and LALR(1) construction, comparing their power, operator-precedence parsing and YACC/Bison.
outcomes: Learners can trace a shift-reduce parse and identify handles
Learners can build LR(0) item sets and SLR tables
Learners can explain LR(1)/LALR(1) lookaheads and merging
Learners can classify a grammar as LR(0), SLR, LALR or CLR

scenes.text: A bottom-up parser stacks tokens and, whenever the top matches a rule's right side, replaces it by the left side.
When only S remains, the input is accepted.

steps.title: Mechanics
steps.body:
Actions: **shift** (push next token), **reduce** (pop a handle β and push A for A → β), **accept**, **error**.
A **handle** is the substring matching a production's RHS whose reduction is one step of the reverse **rightmost derivation**. Bottom-up parsers trace a rightmost derivation in reverse.
Conflicts: **shift/reduce** (e.g. dangling else) and **reduce/reduce**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Trace id * id + id
steps.body:
Grammar E → E + T | T; T → T * F | F; F → id.
$ | id*id+id$ shift → $id reduce F → $F reduce T → $T, sees * → shift → $T* shift id → $T*id reduce F → $T*F reduce T → $T, sees + → reduce E → $E shift + → $E+ shift id → reduce F → T → $E+T reduce E → **accept**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Counting reductions
steps.body: In that trace the reductions were F, T, F, T, E, F, T, E = **8 reductions** (= number of productions used in the rightmost derivation).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reducing T to E before the * is shifted (precedence lost) — the parser must decide using lookahead.
- Treating any RHS match as a handle (must be on the right path of a rightmost derivation).
- Confusing shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts.

activity.prompt: Order the first actions for input id * id with E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → id

quiz.why: A bottom-up parser builds the parse tree from the leaves up, tracing a rightmost derivation in reverse.

options: the RHS reduced in the next reverse rightmost step
quiz.why: A handle is the right-hand side that, when reduced to its left-hand side, takes you one step back in a rightmost derivation.
The dangling else gives a shift/reduce conflict: on seeing else, the parser can reduce the if without else, or shift else.

quiz.q: YACC resolves shift/reduce by default by
quiz.why: YACC resolves a shift/reduce conflict by shifting by default, which matches else with the nearest if.

quiz.q: Actions of a shift-reduce parser include
quiz.why: A shift-reduce parser can shift an input symbol onto the stack, reduce a handle, accept the input, or report an error.

scenes.text: An item A → α•β says: 'I've seen α, I hope to see β'.
Sets of items become the states of a DFA that drives the parser.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body:
Augment: S' → S. **Closure(I):** for each item A → α•Bβ, add B → •γ for all B-productions. **Goto(I, X):** move the dot over X and take the closure. The canonical collection of LR(0) item sets = DFA states.
**LR(0) table:** shift on terminals per goto; reduce A → α in any state containing A → α• on **every** terminal. Conflicts appear easily.
**SLR(1):** reduce A → α only on terminals in **FOLLOW(A)**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · S → AA, A → aA | b
steps.body:
I0: S' → •S, S → •AA, A → •aA, A → •b
I1 = goto(I0, S): S' → S• (accept)
I2 = goto(I0, A): S → A•A, A → •aA, A → •b
I3 = goto(I0, a): A → a•A, A → •aA, A → •b
I4 = goto(I0, b): A → b•
I5 = goto(I2, A): S → AA•
I6 = goto(I3, A): A → aA•
→ **7 states**; no conflicts → the grammar is LR(0) (and SLR).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · SLR conflict
steps.body: S → L = R | R; L → *R | id; R → L. State containing S → L•= R and R → L•: shift on =, and reduce R → L on FOLLOW(R) which contains = → **shift/reduce conflict → not SLR(1)** (it is LALR(1)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to take the closure after goto.
- In SLR, reducing on all terminals (that is LR(0)).
- Missing the augmented production.

activity.prompt: How many LR(0) item sets (states) does the grammar S → AA, A → aA | b have in its canonical collection?

quiz.why: An item with the dot at the end, A → α•, is complete, so it signals a reduce action.
An SLR parser reduces by A → α only when the next input symbol is in FOLLOW(A).

quiz.q: Closure adds items for a variable
quiz.why: Closure adds items for a non-terminal when it appears immediately after the dot, because the parser then expects to see that non-terminal next.
The augmented grammar adds a new start rule S' → S, so the parser has a single accept state.

quiz.q: S → L = R | R with L, R rules is
quiz.why: The grammar S → L = R | R (with L, R) is the textbook example that isn't SLR(1) because of a conflict on '=', but LALR(1) handles it with more precise lookaheads.

scenes.text: LR(1) items carry the token expected after the rule: [A → α•β, a].
LALR merges states with the same core, getting LR(1)-like power with SLR-like size.

steps.title: Canonical LR(1) and LALR(1)
steps.body:
LR(1) item [A → α•Bβ, a]: closure adds [B → •γ, b] for every b ∈ FIRST(βa). Reduce A → α only on its lookahead a. Most powerful of the common LR(1) methods; many states.
**LALR(1):** merge LR(1) states having the same core (same LR(0) items), uniting lookaheads. Number of states = LR(0)/SLR states. Merging can create **reduce/reduce** conflicts but never new shift/reduce conflicts. YACC/Bison produce LALR(1) parsers (Bison also supports canonical LR and GLR).
Power: **LR(0) ⊂ SLR(1) ⊂ LALR(1) ⊂ LR(1)** (as grammar classes). Every LL(1) grammar is LR(1).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · State counts
steps.body: S → CC, C → cC | d: LR(0)/SLR/LALR have **7** states; canonical LR(1) has **10** (states for C → c•C etc. are duplicated with lookaheads {c, d} vs {$}).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Classifying
steps.body:
- S → L = R | R … : not SLR, is LALR.
- S → Aa | bAc | Bc | bBa; A → d; B → d: LR(1) but **not LALR(1)** (merging the states for A → d• and B → d• creates a reduce/reduce conflict).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing LALR has more states than SLR.
- Claiming LALR merging can create shift/reduce conflicts.
- Assuming every LR(1) grammar is LALR(1).

activity.prompt: Match the parser to its property
pairs: Reduces on every terminal in a complete-item state
Merges LR(1) states with equal cores

quiz.q: LALR states equal the number of
quiz.why: LALR merges canonical LR(1) states with identical cores, so it has the same number of states as LR(0) (and SLR).
Merging states in LALR can create reduce/reduce conflicts, since the combined lookahead sets may overlap. It can't create new shift/reduce conflicts.

quiz.q: Most powerful among SLR, LALR, CLR
quiz.why: Canonical LR(1) is the most powerful of the three, because its items carry exact lookaheads. LALR and SLR approximate them.
Every LL(1) grammar is also LR(1). The LR(1) class is strictly larger.

quiz.q: S → CC, C → cC | d canonical LR(1) states
quiz.why: The grammar S → CC, C → cC | d has 10 canonical LR(1) states. The LALR/LR(0) automaton has 7.

scenes.text: For expression grammars, precedence relations ⋖ ≐ ⋗ between operators decide when to reduce.
Real tools like YACC let you declare %left and %right instead.

steps.title: Operator-precedence parsing
steps.body: Works for **operator grammars** (no ε-productions, no two adjacent variables in any RHS). Relations between terminals: a ⋖ b (b has higher precedence: shift), a ≐ b (same handle, e.g. ( ≐ )), a ⋗ b (reduce). Handles are found between ⋖ and ⋗. Simple, but handles few grammars and unary minus is awkward. Precedence functions f, g can compress the table.

steps.title: YACC/Bison
steps.body: Declarations: %token, %left '+' '-' then %left '*' '/' (later lines = higher precedence), %right '^', %nonassoc. Rules with actions { $$ = $1 + $3; }. Precedence/associativity declarations resolve shift/reduce conflicts of ambiguous expression grammars. Lex supplies tokens via yylex().

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Relations
steps.body: For id + id * id with usual precedence: + ⋖ * (shift *), * ⋗ + (reduce first), id ⋗ everything, $ ⋖ everything. So in id + id * id the parser reduces id * id before reducing the +.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Associativity
steps.body: With %left '-', 8 - 3 - 2 parses as (8 - 3) - 2 = **3**; with %right '-' it would be 8 - (3 - 2) = **7**. Exponent is usually %right: 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 = 2 ^ 9 = **512**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using operator precedence parsing for grammars with ε-productions.
- Declaring precedence in the wrong order in YACC (later = higher).
- Forgetting %right for exponentiation.

statements.s: Operator grammars allow two adjacent non-terminals in a RHS.
In YACC, operators declared later have higher precedence.
Operator precedence parsing handles ε-productions easily.
2 ^ 3 ^ 2 with right associativity is 64.

quiz.why: In operator-precedence parsing, a ⋗ b means a has higher precedence than b, so the parser reduces.
YACC generates LALR(1) parsers by default.
Exponentiation (^) is right-associative, so 2^3^2 means 2^(3^2). In YACC, it's declared with %right.
An operator grammar has no ε-productions and no two adjacent non-terminals on a right-hand side.
In YACC, $$ stands for the value of the left-hand side of the rule, which is a synthesised attribute.

questions.q: LR parsers scan input
questions.why: The L in LR means the input is scanned Left to right.

questions.q: Bottom-up parsing produces
questions.why: Bottom-up parsing traces a rightmost derivation in reverse, reducing to the start symbol.

questions.q: YACC default parser
questions.why: YACC (and Bison) generate LALR(1) parsers by default.

questions.q: SLR reduce condition uses
questions.why: An SLR parser decides to reduce A → α only if the next token is in FOLLOW(A).

questions.q: Power ordering
questions.why: The classes nest: LR(0) ⊂ SLR ⊂ LALR ⊂ canonical LR(1), each handling more grammars than the previous one.

questions.q: Ambiguous grammars are LR(k)?
questions.why: An ambiguous grammar is never LR(k), because some conflict can't be avoided. Tools can still use one if precedence declarations resolve the conflicts.

questions.q: Assertion (A): LALR merging cannot create new shift/reduce conflicts. Reason (R): Merged states share the same core, so shift actions are identical and lookaheads only affect reductions. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: LALR merging can't create new shift/reduce conflicts. R is true and explains it: merged states have the same core, so shift actions are identical. Lookaheads affect only reductions, so only reduce/reduce conflicts can appear.

questions.q: LR(0) states for S → AA, A → aA | b
questions.why: The LR(0) automaton for S → AA, A → aA | b has 7 states (I0 to I6). That's the classic count.

questions.q: Number of reductions when parsing id + id with E → E + T | T, T → id
questions.why: The reductions are T → id, E → T, T → id, and E → E + T. That's 4.

questions.q: Case: Bison reports 1 shift/reduce conflict for if-else. Default resolution gives
options: else matched with the nearest if
questions.why: The default is to shift, so the else attaches to the nearest unmatched if, which is the usual meaning.

questions.q: Grammar S → Aa | bAc | Bc | bBa; A → d; B → d is
questions.why: This grammar is LR(1), but merging states in LALR combines the items for A → d and B → d with a mix of lookaheads, giving a reduce/reduce conflict. So it isn't LALR(1).

questions.q: S → CC, C → cC | d: LALR(1) states
questions.why: LALR(1) merges LR(1) states with the same core, so it has the same number of states as LR(0): 7.

questions.q: Is E → E + E | id SLR(1)?
questions.why: E → E + E | id is ambiguous, so it isn't SLR(1): after E + E, with + next, there's a shift/reduce conflict.

questions.q: In an LR(1) item [A → α•, a], reduce on
questions.why: In an LR(1) item [A → α•, a], the parser reduces only when the lookahead is exactly a. SLR uses FOLLOW(A), a coarser set.

questions.q: Which statement is FALSE?
questions.why: The false statement is that every LR(1) grammar is LALR. Some LR(1) grammars aren't LALR(1), because merging creates conflicts. The other statements are true.

questions.q: Precedence: %left '+' then %left '*' then %right '^'. Value of 2 + 3 * 2 ^ 2
questions.why: The precedence is + (lowest), * and then ^ (highest, right-associative). So 2 ^ 2 = 4, then 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Syntax-Directed Translation & Semantic Analysis
courses.summary: Syntax-directed definitions, synthesized and inherited attributes, annotated parse trees and dependency graphs, S-attributed and L-attributed definitions, translation schemes, type expressions and type checking.
outcomes: Learners can evaluate attributes on an annotated parse tree
Learners can classify an SDD as S-attributed or L-attributed
Learners can write a translation scheme for infix-to-postfix
Learners can perform simple type checking with coercions

scenes.text: Every node of a parse tree carries attributes — a value, a type, a piece of code.
Rules attached to productions compute them.

steps.title: Attributes
steps.body:
An **SDD** attaches attributes to grammar symbols and semantic rules to productions.
- **Synthesized** attribute: computed from children (and the node itself) — flows up.
- **Inherited** attribute: computed from parent and/or siblings — flows down/sideways.
**Annotated parse tree:** parse tree with attribute values. **Dependency graph:** edges from attributes to the attributes that use them; evaluate in a **topological order** (cycles = no valid order).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Desk calculator
steps.body:
L → E n { print(E.val) }; E → E₁ + T { E.val = E₁.val + T.val }; E → T; T → T₁ * F { T.val = T₁.val × F.val }; T → F; F → (E); F → digit { F.val = digit.lexval }.
For 3 * 5 + 4: F.val = 3, T.val = 3; F.val = 5 → T.val = 15; E.val = 15; T.val = 4 → E.val = **19**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Inherited attribute
steps.body: Declarations: D → T L { L.inh = T.type }; T → int { T.type = int }; L → L₁ , id { L₁.inh = L.inh; addtype(id, L.inh) }; L → id { addtype(id, L.inh) }. For `int a, b, c`, the type flows from T down into each L → every id gets **int**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling an attribute synthesized when it uses a sibling's value.
- Evaluating attributes in parse order when the dependency graph needs another order.
- Forgetting lexval for terminals (supplied by the lexer).

activity.prompt: Using the desk-calculator SDD, what is E.val for the input 2 * (3 + 4) + 5?

quiz.why: A synthesised attribute at a node is computed from the attributes of its children, so information flows up the tree.
In L-attributed definitions, an inherited attribute may depend on the parent and on left siblings, so information flows down and sideways from left to right.
Attributes must be evaluated in an order consistent with the dependency graph, a topological order, so each value is ready before it's used.

quiz.q: In `int a, b`, b's type is passed as
quiz.why: In a declaration like int a, b, the type int is passed down to each variable name, so b's type is an inherited attribute.

quiz.q: A cycle in the dependency graph means
quiz.why: A cycle in the dependency graph means attributes depend on each other circularly, so there's no valid evaluation order.

scenes.text: An LR parser computes values as it reduces — perfect for synthesized attributes.
A top-down parser can pass information left-to-right — perfect for L-attributed definitions.

steps.title: Classes
steps.body:
- **S-attributed:** only synthesized attributes. Evaluated bottom-up during LR parsing (values kept on the parser stack). Every S-attributed SDD is L-attributed.
- **L-attributed:** each inherited attribute of Xᵢ in A → X₁…Xₙ depends only on inherited attributes of A and attributes of X₁…Xᵢ₋₁ (left siblings), plus Xᵢ itself without cycles. Evaluated in one depth-first, left-to-right traversal (natural for recursive descent / LL parsing).
An SDD where Xᵢ's inherited attribute uses a **right** sibling is **not** L-attributed.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Classify
steps.body:
A → B C { B.i = A.i; C.i = B.s; A.s = C.s } → inherited uses parent and left sibling → **L-attributed** (not S).
A → B C { B.i = C.s; A.s = B.s } → B.i uses its right sibling C → **not L-attributed**.
A → B C { A.s = B.s + C.s } → **S-attributed** (hence L).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Left-recursion removal with attributes
steps.body: E → T R; R → + T R₁ { R₁.i = R.i + T.val; R.s = R₁.s } | ε { R.s = R.i }, with R.i = T.val at the start. For 9 + 5 + 2: R.i flows 9 → 14 → 16, and R.s = **16** comes back up — inherited attributes rebuild left associativity in an LL grammar.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming an S-attributed SDD is not L-attributed.
- Allowing right-sibling dependencies in L-attributed definitions.
- Forgetting that the ε-production must copy the inherited value into the synthesized one.

activity.prompt: Classify each SDD

items.text: A → B C { A.s = B.s × C.s }
A → B C { C.i = B.s; A.s = C.s }
A → B C { B.i = C.s; A.s = B.s }
A → B C { B.i = A.i; A.s = B.s + C.s }
E → E₁ + T { E.v = E₁.v + T.v }

quiz.why: An S-attributed SDD uses only synthesised attributes, so it satisfies the L-attributed rules automatically, as there are no inherited attributes.
S-attributed definitions suit LR (bottom-up) parsing, because the attributes can be computed when each reduction happens.

quiz.q: L-attributed forbids inherited attributes depending on
quiz.why: L-attributed definitions don't allow an inherited attribute to depend on right siblings, because they haven't been evaluated yet in a left-to-right pass.
The translation scheme adds the numbers in turn: 9 + 5 + 2 = 16.

quiz.q: L-attributed SDDs can be evaluated in
quiz.why: L-attributed SDDs can be evaluated in a single left-to-right depth-first traversal of the parse tree.

scenes.text: Put a print statement inside a rule: E → E + T { print('+') }.
Running the parser now converts infix to postfix.

steps.title: SDT schemes
steps.body: A **syntax-directed translation scheme** embeds actions { … } at positions in production bodies; actions execute when the parser reaches that position. Postfix SDTs (actions only at the right end) suit LR parsing. Actions in the middle need marker non-terminals (M → ε) in bottom-up parsers.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Infix to postfix
steps.body:
E → E + T { print('+') } | E − T { print('−') } | T; T → digit { print(digit) }.
For 9 − 5 + 2: the parse tree has + at the root with left child (9 − 5). Depth-first evaluation prints 9 5 − 2 + → **95−2+**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Infix to prefix
steps.body: Moving the actions to the front — E → { print('+') } E + T — prints the operator before the operands: 9 − 5 + 2 → **+−952**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing actions at the wrong position (changes output order).
- Forgetting that embedded actions in LR parsing need markers.
- Assuming the translation of a + b + c is right-associative when the grammar is left-recursive.

activity.prompt: Using the postfix translation scheme, the output for 7 + 3 − 1 is ___

options: at the end of production bodies
quiz.why: In postfix SDT, all actions come at the end of the production bodies, so they run when the parser reduces by that production.
Operators of equal precedence are left-associative, so 9 − 5 + 2 is (9 − 5) + 2, which is 95−2+ in postfix.

quiz.q: Embedded mid-rule actions in LR parsing need
quiz.why: In an LR parser, an action in the middle of a rule is handled by inserting a marker non-terminal M → ε at that point, so a reduction triggers the action.
In a * b + c, the root is +, with a * b as left child and c as right. Prefix writes the operator first: + * a b c.
Semantic actions execute when the parser reaches their position in the production.

scenes.text: `x = 3 + 2.5` mixes an int and a float.
The type checker decides the result type and inserts conversions.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
**Type expressions:** basic (int, float, char, bool, void), constructors (array(n, T), pointer(T), record(...), function T₁ → T₂).
**Type equivalence:** structural (same structure) vs name (same declared name).
**Type checking:** rules like 'if E₁ and E₂ are int then E₁ + E₂ is int'. **Coercion** (implicit widening int → float); **casts** (explicit). Static (compile time: C, Java) vs dynamic (run time: Python) checking; strong vs weak typing.
**Overloading** resolves operators by operand types; **polymorphism** (generic functions).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Widening
steps.body: `float y; int i; y = i * 2 + 1.5;` → i * 2 is int; int + float → coerce to float: t1 = i * 2; t2 = inttofloat(t1); t3 = t2 + 1.5; y = t3.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Function types
steps.body: `int f(float, char*)` has type (float × pointer(char)) → int. The call f(3, "a") type-checks after coercing 3 to float.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming name and structural equivalence always agree.
- Narrowing implicitly (float → int loses data; C allows it with a warning).
- Confusing dynamic typing with weak typing (Python is dynamic and strong).

activity.prompt: Match the concept
pairs: Implicit conversion such as int → float
Same operator name, different operand types

quiz.why: In C, int + float is converted by widening the int to float, so the result type is float.
Python is dynamically typed (types are checked at run time) and strongly typed (no silent mixing of types such as str + int).
The type of int a[10] is built with the array constructor: array(10, int).

quiz.q: Type checking at compile time is
quiz.why: Type checking done at compile time is static type checking.
A function type is written domain → range, so int g(char) has type char → int.

questions.q: Synthesized attributes flow
questions.why: Synthesised attributes are computed from a node's children, so they flow up the tree.

questions.q: S-attributed SDDs use
questions.why: An S-attributed SDD uses only synthesised attributes.

questions.q: Coercion is
questions.why: Coercion is an implicit type conversion made by the compiler, such as converting an int to a float.

questions.q: Desk calculator value of 2 + 3 * 4
questions.why: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.

questions.q: Infix a − b − c to postfix (left assoc)
questions.why: Subtraction is left-associative, so a − b − c = (a − b) − c, which in postfix is ab−c−.

questions.q: Every S-attributed SDD is L-attributed?
questions.why: Yes. S-attributed SDDs have no inherited attributes at all, so they satisfy the L-attributed conditions trivially.

questions.q: Assertion (A): L-attributed SDDs can be evaluated during LL parsing. Reason (R): Attribute information flows only from left to right and top-down. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: L-attributed SDDs can be evaluated during LL (top-down) parsing. R is true and explains it: attributes flow only top-down and left to right, matching how an LL parser proceeds.

questions.q: A → B C { C.i = A.i; B.i = C.s; A.s = B.s }. Classification
questions.why: B.i = C.s uses the synthesised attribute of C, a right sibling of B. L-attributed rules forbid that, so it isn't L-attributed.

questions.q: Postfix translation of (2 + 3) * 4
questions.why: The parentheses force 2 + 3 to be done first. Postfix writes operands then operator: 2 3 + 4 *.

questions.q: Case: a student's compiler accepts `int x = "hello";` silently. Which phase is missing a check?
questions.why: Assigning a string to an int is a type mismatch. It's the semantic analysis phase's type checking that should have rejected it.

questions.q: Prefix translation of 9 − 5 + 2
questions.why: 9 − 5 + 2 is (9 − 5) + 2. The root is +, with left child 9 − 5 and right child 2. In prefix: + − 9 5 2.

questions.q: With R.i inherited for E → T R, R → + T R₁, the value for 1 + 2 + 3 + 4
questions.why: The inherited attribute carries the running sum along: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

questions.q: Structural equivalence: type A = array(5, int), B = array(5, int) declared separately. Equivalent under name equivalence?
questions.why: Under name equivalence, types are the same only if they have the same name. A and B are declared separately, so they differ, even though their structure matches.

questions.q: Desk-calculator SDD evaluates (1 + 2) * (3 + 4) * 2
questions.why: (1 + 2) = 3 and (3 + 4) = 7, so the product is 3 × 7 × 2 = 42.

questions.q: Translation scheme E → E₁ + T { E.code = E₁.code || T.code || '+' } generates
questions.why: E.code = E₁.code || T.code || '+' puts the operator after its operands, which is postfix notation.

questions.q: Which dependency makes an SDD circular?
options: A.s = B.s; B.i = A.s with B.s depending on B.i
questions.why: A.s depends on B.s, B.i depends on A.s, and B.s depends on B.i. That's a cycle A.s → B.i → B.s → A.s, so the SDD is circular.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Intermediate Code Generation
courses.summary: Syntax trees and DAGs, three-address code, quadruples, triples and indirect triples, SSA basics, translating expressions, array references, Boolean expressions and control flow, and backpatching.
outcomes: Learners can draw syntax trees and DAGs and count nodes
Learners can generate three-address code for expressions and arrays
Learners can represent code as quadruples and triples
Learners can translate if/while with jumps and backpatching

lessons.title: Syntax trees, DAGs and three-address code

scenes.text: In a = b * -c + b * -c the same subexpression appears twice.
A DAG stores it once, and the code computes it once.

steps.title: Representations
steps.body:
- **Syntax tree:** operators as interior nodes, operands as leaves.
- **DAG:** like a syntax tree but identical subexpressions share one node (value-number method: reuse a node with the same operator and children).
- **Three-address code (TAC):** at most one operator on the RHS: x = y op z, x = op y, x = y, goto L, if x relop y goto L, param x, call p, n, x = y[i], x[i] = y, x = &y, x = *y.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Tree vs DAG
steps.body:
a = b * −c + b * −c.
- TAC from the syntax tree: t1 = minus c; t2 = b * t1; t3 = minus c; t4 = b * t3; t5 = t2 + t4; a = t5.
- TAC from the DAG: t1 = minus c; t2 = b * t1; t3 = t2 + t2; a = t3.
The syntax tree has 11 nodes (=, a, +, *, b, minus, c, *, b, minus, c); the DAG has **7** (=, a, +, *, b, minus, c) because the repeated b * −c is shared.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Temporaries
steps.body: x = (a + b) * (a + b) − c: DAG shares a + b → t1 = a + b; t2 = t1 * t1; t3 = t2 − c; x = t3 → **3 temporaries**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sharing nodes whose operand values may have changed in between (DAGs are built per basic block).
- Writing two operators in one TAC instruction.
- Forgetting unary minus is an operator.

activity.prompt: Generate three-address code from a postfix expression (single-letter operands, binary operators + - * /). Print one instruction per line using temporaries t1, t2, …
activity.starter:
tokens = input().split()
stack = []
count = 0
# operands: push; operator: pop two, emit 'tK = left op right', push tK
activity.solution:
tokens = input().split()
stack = []
count = 0
for tk in tokens:
    if tk in '+-*/':
        right = stack.pop()
        left = stack.pop()
        count += 1
        t = 't' + str(count)
        print(t, '=', left, tk, right)
        stack.append(t)
    else:
        stack.append(tk)
activity.hint: Pop the right operand first.

quiz.q: TAC allows how many operators on the RHS?
quiz.why: Three-address code has at most one operator on the right-hand side, hence three addresses: two operands and a result.
A DAG of a basic block shares nodes for common subexpressions, so repeated computations are noticed and done once.

quiz.q: TAC for x = a + b * c needs how many temporaries (one per operator)?
quiz.why: x = a + b * c takes t1 = b * c, then t2 = a + t1, then x = t2 (or merged). That's 2 temporaries, one per operator.
Three-address code has a unary form such as x = minus y for negation.
DAGs are usually built for basic blocks, straight-line code, to find common subexpressions in them.

scenes.text: An optimiser needs to move and rewrite instructions.
How TAC is stored — quadruples, triples or indirect triples — decides how easy that is.

steps.title: Representations
steps.body:
- **Quadruples:** (op, arg1, arg2, result) — explicit temporaries; easy to reorder.
- **Triples:** (op, arg1, arg2), results referred to by position (0), (1)… — saves space; moving instructions breaks references.
- **Indirect triples:** a list of pointers to triples — reordering changes only the pointer list.
- **SSA (static single assignment):** each variable assigned exactly once (x1, x2…); φ-functions merge values at join points; simplifies many optimisations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using variable names instead of positions in triples.
- Forgetting that reordering triples requires renumbering references.
- Thinking SSA forbids reassigning at run time (it is a naming discipline; loops still execute repeatedly).

activity.prompt: Match the representation
pairs: Separate list of pointers to triples
Each variable assigned once; φ at joins

quiz.why: Quadruples name each result explicitly, and indirect triples reorder through a pointer list, so instructions are easy to move.
Triples have no result field: an instruction's result is referred to by its position, so they use less space.
φ-functions are used in SSA form to merge values from different control-flow paths.
A quadruple has four fields: operator, argument 1, argument 2 and result.
In triples, the reference (2) means the result of the instruction at position 2.

lessons.title: Arrays, Boolean expressions and control flow

scenes.text: Machine code has no if or while — only comparisons and jumps.
The translator lays out labels and jumps for each construct.

steps.title: Array addressing
steps.body:
1-D: addr(A[i]) = base + (i − low) × w.
2-D row-major (C): addr(A[i][j]) = base + ((i − low₁) × n₂ + (j − low₂)) × w, n₂ = number of columns. Column-major (Fortran): base + ((j − low₂) × n₁ + (i − low₁)) × w.

steps.title: Control flow
steps.body:
if (B) S1 else S2:
  code for B with true → L1, false → L2
  L1: S1; goto Lnext
  L2: S2
  Lnext:
while (B) S: Lbegin: B (false → Lnext); S; goto Lbegin; Lnext:
**Short-circuit** Booleans: B1 || B2 → if B1 true jump to true; else evaluate B2. B1 && B2 → if B1 false jump to false.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · while loop
steps.body:
while (i < n) { s = s + i; i = i + 1; }
L1: if i < n goto L2
    goto L3
L2: s = s + i
    i = i + 1
    goto L1
L3:

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rows instead of columns for n₂ in row-major formulas.
- Forgetting the lower bound when it is not 0.
- Evaluating both operands of && when the first is false (short-circuit semantics).

activity.prompt: int A[5][8] row-major, element size 4 bytes, base 2000, indices from 0. Address of A[2][3]?

quiz.why: The address of A[i][j] in row-major order is base + (i × columns + j) × width, so it uses the number of columns to skip i whole rows.

quiz.q: Short-circuit for a && b: if a is false
options: jump to false without evaluating b
quiz.why: For a && b, if a is false the whole expression is false, so the code jumps straight to the false branch without evaluating b.
A while loop jumps back to the test at the end of the body, so its translation needs a backward jump.

quiz.q: A[1..10] of 4-byte ints, base 500: address of A[4]
quiz.why: Address of A[4] = base + (index − lower bound) × width = 500 + (4 − 1) × 4 = 512.
Fortran (and MATLAB) store arrays in column-major order. C and Python lists are row-major.

scenes.text: When writing a jump for an if, you don't yet know where the else part starts.
Leave a blank, keep a list of blanks, and fill them in later — backpatching.

steps.title: Technique
steps.body:
One-pass translation of jumps: B.truelist and B.falselist hold indices of incomplete jump instructions; makelist(i), merge(p1, p2), backpatch(p, i) fills target i into every instruction in p. Marker M → ε { M.instr = nextinstr }.
- B → B₁ || M B₂: backpatch(B₁.falselist, M.instr); B.truelist = merge(B₁.truelist, B₂.truelist); B.falselist = B₂.falselist.
- B → B₁ && M B₂: backpatch(B₁.truelist, M.instr); B.truelist = B₂.truelist; B.falselist = merge(B₁.falselist, B₂.falselist).
- B → E₁ relop E₂: truelist = makelist(nextinstr), falselist = makelist(nextinstr + 1); emit 'if E₁ relop E₂ goto _' and 'goto _'.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · x < 100 || x > 200 && x != y
steps.body:
Starting at instruction 100:
100: if x < 100 goto _
101: goto _ (→ 102)
102: if x > 200 goto _ (→ 104)
103: goto _
104: if x != y goto _
105: goto _
Backpatching: 101 → 102 (|| falselist), 102 → 104 (&& truelist). Truelist = {100, 104}; falselist = {103, 105}.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · if-then
steps.body:
if (a < b) x = 1;
200: if a < b goto 202
201: goto 203
202: x = 1
203: … (falselist backpatched to 203 once S's end is known)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Backpatching the || truelist instead of the falselist with M.instr.
- Losing incomplete jumps by not merging lists.
- Forgetting that && and || differ in which list is patched.

statements.s: For B₁ || B₂, B₁.falselist is backpatched to the start of B₂.
statements.why: If B₁ is false, try B₂.

statements.s: For B₁ && B₂, B₁.falselist is backpatched to the start of B₂.
Backpatching allows one-pass generation of jump targets.
A relational expression creates two incomplete jumps.
merge(p1, p2) fills in jump targets.

quiz.why: makelist(i) creates a new list containing just the instruction index i, to be filled in later.
For B₁ && B₂, the expression is false if either is false, so falselist = merge(B₁.falselist, B₂.falselist).
The marker M records the index of the next instruction to be generated, so backpatch lists can be filled in with it.

quiz.q: In the example, truelist after parsing
quiz.why: In the worked example, the jumps that go to the true target are the instructions at 100 and 104, so the truelist is {100, 104}.

quiz.q: Backpatching is needed because targets are
options: unknown when the jump is emitted
quiz.why: Backpatching is needed because forward jump targets aren't known when the jump is emitted. They are filled in later.

questions.q: TAC instruction count for x = a + b + c (one per operator, plus copy merged)
questions.why: x = a + b + c needs t1 = a + b and then x = t1 + c, which is 2 instructions.

questions.q: Quadruple has
questions.why: A quadruple has 4 fields: op, arg1, arg2 and result.

questions.q: DAG eliminates
questions.why: A DAG shares nodes for identical subexpressions, so common subexpressions are computed only once.

questions.q: Row-major A[i][j] needs
questions.why: In row-major order the address of A[i][j] depends on the number of columns, to skip whole rows.

questions.q: Indirect triples allow
questions.why: Indirect triples keep a separate list of pointers to triples, so the order can be changed by reordering the pointer list.

questions.q: SSA uses
questions.why: SSA (static single assignment) form uses φ-functions at merge points to pick between values from different paths.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Triples are hard to reorder. Reason (R): Results are referenced by instruction position. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: triples are hard to reorder. R is true and explains it: results are referenced by position, so moving an instruction changes the references to it.

questions.q: int A[10][10], 2-byte elements, base 100, row-major from 0: address of A[5][6]
questions.why: Row-major address = base + (i × columns + j) × width = 100 + (5 × 10 + 6) × 2 = 100 + 112 = 212.

questions.q: DAG node count for a + a * (b − c) + (b − c) * d (leaves a, b, c, d shared)
questions.why: Leaves a, b, c, d (4); b − c (1, shared); a * (b − c) (1); (b − c) * d (1); the two + nodes (2) → 9.

questions.q: Case: an optimiser moves instruction (3) earlier in a triple list and the code breaks. Better representation
questions.why: Moving a triple changes the position numbers that other triples refer to. Quadruples (named results) or indirect triples (a pointer list) give stable references.

questions.q: Column-major A[1..4][1..5], w = 4, base 0: address of A[2][3]
questions.why: Column-major address = base + ((col − 1) × rows + (row − 1)) × width = ((3 − 1) × 4 + (2 − 1)) × 4 = (8 + 1) × 4 = 36.

questions.q: Temporaries for x = (a + b) * (c + d) − (a + b) using a DAG
questions.why: The DAG shares a + b: t1 = a + b, t2 = c + d, t3 = t1 * t2, x = t3 − t1. So 3 temporaries are used before the final assignment.

questions.q: Backpatching B₁ || M B₂: which list of B₁ gets M.instr
questions.why: For B₁ || B₂, B₂ is evaluated only if B₁ is false, so B₁'s falselist is backpatched with M.instr (the start of B₂).

questions.q: For `if (a < b && c < d) x = 1;` starting at 100, how many conditional/unconditional jumps are emitted for the condition?
questions.why: Each relational test emits a conditional jump (if-goto) and an unconditional goto, so two relops give 4 jumps.

questions.q: SSA form of x = 1; x = x + 2; y = x
questions.why: In SSA every assignment gets a new name: x₁ = 1; x₂ = x₁ + 2; y₁ = x₂.

questions.q: TAC for x = y[i] uses
questions.why: Three-address code has the indexed copy form x = y[i], which is one of the allowed instruction forms.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Run-Time Environments & Symbol Tables
courses.summary: Storage organisation, activation records and the control stack, static vs dynamic scoping, access links and displays, parameter-passing methods, heap management and garbage collection, and symbol-table organisation.
outcomes: Learners can draw the activation records of a call sequence
Learners can predict outputs under static and dynamic scoping
Learners can predict outputs under call by value, reference, value-result and name
Learners can compare garbage-collection approaches and symbol-table structures

scenes.text: Each function call places a tray (activation record) on the stack; returning removes it.
The tray holds parameters, locals, the return address and links.

steps.title: Memory layout
steps.body:
Code | static data (globals) | heap (grows up) … stack (grows down).
**Activation record (frame):** actual parameters, returned value, **control link** (caller's frame), **access link** (for non-local data under static scoping), saved machine status (return address, registers), local data, temporaries.
**Calling sequence** split between caller (evaluate args, push, save return address) and callee (save registers, allocate locals). Recursion needs stack allocation; Fortran 77 could use static allocation (no recursion).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Recursion depth
steps.body: fact(4) calls fact(3) … fact(0): at the deepest point the stack holds **5** activation records for fact (plus main).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Fibonacci call count
steps.body: Naive fib(n) with fib(0) = fib(1) base cases: calls(n) = calls(n − 1) + calls(n − 2) + 1, calls(0) = calls(1) = 1. calls(5) = **15**; maximum stack depth = 5 records of fib (fib(5) → fib(4) → … → fib(1)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing the control link (dynamic chain) with the access link (static chain).
- Thinking heap and stack data are freed the same way.
- Assuming static allocation supports recursion.

activity.prompt: Naive recursive fib with base cases fib(0) and fib(1): how many calls in total for fib(6)?

quiz.why: The control link in an activation record points to the caller's activation record (the dynamic chain), so control can return there.
Access links form the static chain, which lets a nested procedure reach non-local variables under static scoping.
Recursion has several live calls to the same function at once, so each needs its own frame, allocated on a stack (or heap).

quiz.q: Locals of a function normally live in
quiz.why: Local variables normally live in the function's stack frame (activation record), which is created at the call and removed at return.

quiz.q: Max frames for fact(6) (fact(0) base) excluding main
quiz.why: The deepest chain is fact(6), fact(5), …, fact(0), which gives 7 frames alive at once.

scenes.text: A function prints x — but there are two variables named x: a global and a local in its caller.
Static scoping looks where the function is written; dynamic scoping looks at who called it.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- **Static (lexical) scoping:** a name refers to the nearest enclosing declaration in the program text (C, Java, Python). Implemented with access links or a **display** (array of pointers to the most recent frame at each nesting depth).
- **Dynamic scoping:** a name refers to the most recent active binding at run time (early Lisp, Bash local variables, Perl's local). Implemented with deep access (search the control stack) or shallow access (central table).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Classic
Solved example 2 · Nested procedures
steps.body: In a language with nested functions (Pascal-like), procedure q nested in p accesses p's local y via one access-link hop; a procedure nested two levels deeper needs two hops (or one display lookup).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the caller's variables under static scoping.
- Thinking dynamic scoping is resolved at compile time.
- Forgetting the display must be saved/restored on calls.

a.text: Code: int x = 10; void show() { print(x); } void run() { int x = 20; show(); } main() { run(); }. Under STATIC scoping what is printed?

choices.feedback: Correct: show() was written where the global x is visible.

a2.text: Static scoping looks at where show() is defined, not who called it. Inside show, the nearest enclosing x in the text is the global (10).

b.text: Now the same program under DYNAMIC scoping. What is printed?

choices.feedback: Correct: the most recent active binding of x is run()'s local.
Under dynamic scoping run()'s x = 20 is still active when show runs.

end.text: Static: 10. Dynamic: 20. Most modern languages (C, Java, Python, JavaScript) use static scoping.

quiz.why: C uses static (lexical) scoping: a name refers to the declaration visible in the program text.

quiz.q: Under dynamic scoping a free variable is resolved by
quiz.why: Under dynamic scoping, a free variable is resolved at run time to the most recent active binding on the call stack.

options: an array of frame pointers per nesting level
quiz.why: A display is an array of frame pointers, one for each nesting level, which gives fast access to non-local variables.
Static scoping resolves the name to the global in both calls, so both outputs are 1.

options: the symbol table at compile time
quiz.why: Deep access implements dynamic scoping by searching down the control stack for the most recent binding of the name.

scenes.text: Photocopy (value), the original notebook (reference), or a copy returned at the end (value-result)?
Each choice changes what the caller sees afterwards.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- **Call by value:** formal gets a copy; changes do not affect the actual (C, Java primitives).
- **Call by reference:** formal is an alias of the actual's location (C++ &, Pascal var).
- **Call by value-result (copy-in copy-out):** copy in at call, copy back at return (Ada in out for scalars).
- **Call by name:** actual expression is re-evaluated each time the formal is used, in the caller's environment (Algol 60; like macro substitution with thunks). Lazy evaluation (Haskell) is call by need.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Same call, four answers
steps.body:
void f(int x, int y) { x = x + 1; y = y + x; }  main: a = 1; f(a, a); print(a).
- **Value:** a = **1**.
- **Reference:** x, y alias a: a = 2, then a = 2 + 2 = **4**.
- **Value-result** (copy back x then y): x = 2, y = 1 + 2 = 3; copy x → a = 2, copy y → a = **3**.
- **Name:** x and y both mean a → same as reference here: **4**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · swap by name fails
steps.body: swap(i, A[i]) by name with temp = i; i = A[i]; A[i] = temp: with i = 1, A[1] = 3 → temp = 1; i = 3; A[i] means A[3] = 1 → A[1] stays 3 — the swap goes wrong because A[i] is re-evaluated after i changed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Java passes objects by reference (it passes references by value).
- Forgetting the copy-back order in value-result.
- Treating call by name as call by reference (they differ when expressions involve changing variables).

activity.prompt: void g(int p) { p = p * 2; } with call by reference: a = 5; g(a); g(a); print(a). What is printed?

quiz.why: Java passes everything by value. For objects, the value copied is the reference, so the callee can change the object but not the caller's variable.
In call by value-result, the formals are copied in at the call, and their final values are copied back to the actuals at return.

quiz.q: Call by name re-evaluates the argument
options: each time the formal is used
quiz.why: Call by name re-evaluates the argument expression every time the formal parameter is used, via a thunk.

quiz.q: f(a, a) by reference in example 1 prints
quiz.why: With call by reference both parameters alias the same variable a, so updates through one are seen by the other. The result in the example is 4.
In C++, int& declares a reference parameter, so the function works on the caller's variable directly: call by reference.

lessons.title: Heap management, garbage collection and symbol tables

scenes.text: Objects created with new live on the heap until no one needs them.
A garbage collector finds unreachable objects and frees them.

steps.title: Heap and GC
steps.body:
Allocation: free lists, first/best fit, buddy system (blocks of 2ᵏ), fragmentation. Manual (malloc/free) risks dangling pointers and leaks.
Garbage collection:
- **Reference counting:** free when count = 0; immediate; cannot reclaim **cycles**.
- **Mark-and-sweep:** mark from roots, sweep unmarked; handles cycles; pause.
- **Copying (semi-space):** copy live objects to the other half; compacts; uses 2× space.
- **Generational:** most objects die young; collect the nursery often (Java, .NET).
- Mark-compact, incremental/concurrent collectors reduce pauses.

steps.title: Symbol tables
steps.body: Store name, type, scope level, storage location, size, line of declaration. Structures: linear list (O(n) lookup), **hash table** (O(1) average — most common), search trees. Scopes: a stack of tables or one table with scope numbers; entering a block pushes, leaving pops.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Reference-counting cycle
steps.body: Objects A and B point to each other; the program drops its only reference to A. Counts: A = 1 (from B), B = 1 (from A) → never 0 → **leak** under pure reference counting; a tracing collector frees both.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Buddy system
steps.body: Request 70 KB from a 512 KB block: split 512 → 256 + 256 → 128 + 128; allocate a **128 KB** block (internal fragmentation 58 KB). Freeing it lets buddies merge back.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming reference counting handles cycles.
- Thinking copying collectors need no extra space.
- Using linear lists for large symbol tables.

activity.prompt: Match the GC technique to its trait
pairs: Traces from roots, then frees unmarked
Compacts by copying live objects; needs extra space

quiz.why: Hash tables are the most common symbol-table structure, since they give fast, average O(1) lookup.
Reference counting can't reclaim cycles: objects that point to each other keep each other's counts above zero.

options: half the heap at a time
quiz.why: A copying collector uses two semi-spaces and works in one half at a time, copying live objects to the other.
A dangling pointer arises when memory is freed while a pointer to it is still used.

quiz.q: Buddy allocation for a 33 KB request from 64 KB
quiz.why: A buddy allocator hands out blocks in power-of-two sizes. For 33 KB the next size up is 64 KB, so it gets a 64 KB block.

questions.q: Activation records live on the
questions.why: Activation records are normally kept on the control stack.

questions.q: C uses ___ scoping
questions.why: C uses static (lexical) scoping.

questions.q: Reference counting cannot free
questions.why: Reference counting can't free cycles, since objects in a cycle keep each other's counts above zero.

questions.q: Control link points to
questions.why: The control link points to the caller's frame, which is where control returns.

questions.q: Call by value: changes to the formal
questions.why: In call by value the formal is a copy, so changing it doesn't affect the caller's actual argument.

questions.q: Hash-table symbol lookup average
questions.why: Hash-table lookup takes O(1) time on average.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Copying collectors eliminate fragmentation. Reason (R): Live objects are copied contiguously into the other semi-space. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: copying collectors eliminate fragmentation. R is true and explains it: live objects are copied contiguously into the other semi-space, which compacts them.

questions.q: void f(int x) { x = x + 10; } a = 5; f(a); print(a) with value-result
questions.why: The formal x starts as a copy of 5, becomes 15, and at return the value 15 is copied back to a. So a is 15.

questions.q: Calls of naive fib(4) (base fib(0), fib(1))
Case: a long-running Python server leaks memory with two objects referencing each other. CPython reclaims them because
options: its cycle detector supplements reference counting
questions.why: CPython uses reference counting, which can't free cycles by itself, so it adds a cycle detector (the gc module) that finds and collects such cycles.

questions.q: int x = 5; f() { x = x + 1; } g() { int x = 10; f(); print(x); } main() { g(); print(x); } under dynamic scoping prints
questions.why: With dynamic scoping, f's x refers to the most recent binding, g's local x = 10. f makes it 11, so g prints 11. The global x is untouched and main prints 5.

questions.q: Same program under static scoping prints
questions.why: With static scoping, f's x is the global one, so f makes the global 6. g's local x is still 10, so g prints 10, and main prints 6.

questions.q: f(x, y) { y = y + 1; x = x + y; } a = 2; f(a, a); print a. Call by reference
questions.why: By reference, x and y are both aliases of a. y = y + 1 makes a = 3, then x = x + y = 3 + 3 = 6. So a prints 6.

questions.q: Same call by value-result (copy back x then y)
questions.why: Value-result: x = 2 and y = 2 are copies. y = 3, then x = 2 + 3 = 5. At return, x is copied to a (a = 5), then y is copied to a (a = 3). So a ends as 3.

questions.q: Buddy system: requests 60 KB and 130 KB from 512 KB. Total internal fragmentation
questions.why: 60 KB gets a 64 KB block (4 KB wasted); 130 KB gets a 256 KB block (126 KB wasted) → 130 KB in total.

questions.q: Display depth for a procedure at nesting level 3 accessing level-1 data
questions.why: A display keeps a pointer to the frame at each nesting level, so reaching level-1 data takes one display lookup, with no chain-following or search.
