courses.title: Unit 7 · Code Optimisation & Code Generation
courses.summary: Basic blocks and flow graphs, local optimisations with DAGs, loop optimisations, data-flow analysis (reaching definitions, live variables, available expressions), register allocation by graph colouring, instruction selection, and peephole optimisation.
outcomes: Learners can partition code into basic blocks and draw a flow graph
Learners can apply constant folding, CSE, copy propagation and dead-code elimination
Learners can compute liveness and reaching definitions
Learners can allocate registers by colouring an interference graph

scenes.text: A basic block is a straight road: enter at the start, leave at the end, no turns in between.
The flow graph is the road map joining blocks.

steps.title: Leaders
steps.body:
Leaders: (1) the first instruction; (2) any target of a jump; (3) any instruction immediately after a jump. Each block runs from a leader up to (not including) the next leader.
Flow graph: edge B1 → B2 if B2 can follow B1 (fall-through or jump). A **loop** has a header that dominates all nodes in it; a **back edge** goes to a dominator. **Dominator:** d dominates n if every path from entry to n goes through d.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Find the blocks
steps.body:
1: i = 1
2: j = 1
3: t1 = 10 * i
4: t2 = t1 + j
5: j = j + 1
6: if j <= 10 goto 3
7: i = i + 1
8: if i <= 10 goto 2
9: halt
Leaders: 1 (first), 2 (target), 3 (target), 7 (after jump), 9 (after jump). Blocks: B1 {1}, B2 {2}, B3 {3–6}, B4 {7–8}, B5 {9} → **5 blocks**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Edges
steps.body: B1 → B2, B2 → B3, B3 → B3 (back edge), B3 → B4, B4 → B2 (back edge), B4 → B5 → two natural loops: inner {B3}, outer {B2, B3, B4}.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that the instruction after a conditional jump is a leader.
- Splitting blocks at every assignment.
- Treating any cycle edge as a back edge without checking dominance.

activity.prompt: Code: 1: a = 0; 2: if a > 5 goto 6; 3: b = a * 2; 4: a = a + 1; 5: goto 2; 6: print b. How many basic blocks?

quiz.why: The instruction immediately after a jump (conditional or unconditional) is a leader, because control reaches it as the start of a new basic block.

options: enters only at the start and leaves only at the end
quiz.why: A basic block is straight-line code: control enters only at the first instruction and leaves only at the last.
A back edge goes to a dominator, the loop header, so it identifies a natural loop.
Every path from the entry starts at the entry node, so it dominates every node in the flow graph.
The leaders at lines 1, 2, 3, 7 and 9 start 5 basic blocks.

scenes.text: Compute once, reuse; fold constants at compile time; drop code nobody uses.
Inside loops, every saved instruction is saved thousands of times.

steps.title: Machine-independent optimisations
steps.body:
- **Constant folding/propagation:** x = 2 * 3 → 6; replace uses of a known constant.
- **Common subexpression elimination (CSE):** reuse a computed value (DAG within a block; available expressions globally).
- **Copy propagation:** after x = y, use y for x.
- **Dead-code elimination:** remove statements whose results are never used.
- **Loop-invariant code motion:** move computations that don't change in the loop to a preheader.
- **Strength reduction:** replace expensive ops (i * 4) by cheaper ones (t = t + 4).
- **Induction-variable elimination**, **loop unrolling**, **loop fusion/jamming**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Chain of optimisations
steps.body:
Before: x = 4; y = x * 2; z = a + b; w = a + b; v = y + 1; (z unused later)
- Constant propagation/folding: y = 8; v = 9
- CSE: w = z → copy propagation uses z
- Dead code: if x, y, z are not used later, their assignments go → only the needed results remain.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Strength reduction
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Moving code out of a loop when it is not invariant or when the loop may run zero times and the code has side effects.
- Eliminating 'dead' code that has side effects (I/O, volatile).
- CSE across a redefinition of an operand.

activity.prompt: Name the optimisation

items.text: Move t = n * 4 above a loop that never changes n
Replace i * 8 in a loop by t = t + 8
Delete y = a + b when y is never used

quiz.q: Replacing x * 2 by x + x is
quiz.why: Replacing a multiplication by an addition (x * 2 → x + x) is strength reduction: using a cheaper operation.

options: are not redefined between the uses
quiz.why: Common-subexpression elimination is only valid if the operands haven't been redefined between the two uses, so both give the same value.
Loop unrolling makes the code bigger but cuts the number of loop-control branches and tests.

options: code whose results are never used
quiz.why: Dead code is code whose results are never used, so it can be removed without changing the program's behaviour.

quiz.q: Code motion moves invariant code to the
quiz.why: Code motion moves loop-invariant computations out to the loop preheader, so they run once instead of on every iteration.

scenes.text: Which definitions can reach this line? Which variables will be used later?
Data-flow equations propagate such facts around the flow graph until nothing changes.

steps.title: Three classic analyses
steps.body:
- **Reaching definitions (forward, union):** OUT[B] = gen[B] ∪ (IN[B] − kill[B]); IN[B] = ∪ OUT[preds]. Used for constant propagation, use-def chains.
- **Live variables (backward, union):** IN[B] = use[B] ∪ (OUT[B] − def[B]); OUT[B] = ∪ IN[succs]. A variable is live at a point if its current value may be used later. Used for register allocation and dead-code elimination.
- **Available expressions (forward, intersection):** expression available if computed on every path and operands not redefined since. Used for global CSE.
Iterate until a fixed point.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Liveness in a block
steps.body:
Block: a = b + c; d = a − e; b = d * 2; (b and d live on exit).
Backward: after the last statement live = {b, d}; b = d * 2 kills b, uses d → {d}; d = a − e kills d, uses a, e → {a, e}; a = b + c kills a, uses b, c → {b, c, e}. **Live on entry = {b, c, e}**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Reaching definitions
steps.body: d1: x = 1 (B1); d2: x = 2 (B2, inside an if); B3 joins both. IN[B3] = {d1, d2} → x is **not** a constant at B3. If only d1 reached, constant propagation could replace x by 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Running liveness forward (it is backward).
- Using intersection for reaching definitions (it is union; available expressions use intersection).
- Forgetting that a use before a definition in the same block makes the variable live on entry.

activity.prompt: Block: x = y + z; y = x * 2; w = y + 1 with only w live on exit. Live variables on entry (alphabetical, comma separated): ___

quiz.why: Liveness analysis works backward: a variable is live if it will be used later, so you propagate information from uses back to earlier points.
Reaching definitions uses union at merge points, since a definition reaches if it reaches along any path.
Available expressions uses intersection, since an expression is available only if it's computed along every path.
Liveness information is used for register allocation, as two variables live at the same time can't share a register.
IN[B] = use[B] ∪ (OUT[B] − def[B]): variables used in B, plus those live out that B doesn't redefine.

lessons.title: Register allocation, instruction selection and peephole

scenes.text: A CPU has only a few registers but programs have many variables.
Variables alive at the same time can't share — colour the interference graph.

steps.title: Code generation issues
steps.body:
- **Instruction selection:** map IR to target instructions (tree tiling, maximal munch), using addressing modes well.
- **Register allocation:** build the **interference graph** (edge if two variables are live at the same time); colour with k = number of registers; if impossible, **spill** some to memory. Chaitin's heuristic: repeatedly remove nodes with degree < k.
- **Instruction scheduling** to avoid pipeline stalls.
- **Peephole optimisation** on small windows: redundant load/store removal (MOV R0, a; MOV a, R0), jumps to jumps, unreachable code, algebraic simplification (x + 0, x * 1), strength reduction, using machine idioms (INC).
Sethi–Ullman numbering gives the minimum registers to evaluate an expression tree without spills.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Colouring
steps.body: Live ranges: a and b overlap, b and c overlap, c and d overlap, a and c overlap. Interference graph edges: a–b, b–c, c–d, a–c → triangle a, b, c → needs **3 colours**; d can reuse a's colour. With only 2 registers, one variable must be spilled.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Peephole
steps.body:
MOV R0, a
MOV a, R0  ← redundant store (a already equals R0), delete
GOTO L1
L1: GOTO L2  ← jump to jump → replace first with GOTO L2
ADD R1, #0  ← algebraic identity, delete

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding interference edges between variables that are never live together.
- Forgetting spill code costs (loads/stores).
- Deleting a 'redundant' store when a label (jump target) sits between the two instructions.

activity.prompt: Interference graph: edges a–b, a–c, a–d, b–c, b–d, c–d (all four variables mutually live). Minimum number of registers without spilling?

quiz.q: Interference edge means two variables are
quiz.why: An interference edge joins two variables that are live at the same time, so they must be in different registers.

quiz.q: If the graph needs more colours than registers
quiz.why: If the interference graph needs more colours than there are registers, some variables are spilled to memory.
Peephole optimisation looks at a small window of instructions and replaces patterns with better ones.

quiz.q: Jump to a jump is replaced by
options: a direct jump to the final target
quiz.why: A jump to a jump can be replaced with a direct jump to the final target, saving a step.

quiz.q: Graph colouring register allocation is due to
quiz.why: Graph-colouring register allocation is the classic approach by Chaitin and colleagues.

questions.q: A basic block has
questions.why: A basic block has a single entry point and a single exit point, with no jumps in between.

questions.q: Constant folding happens at
questions.why: Constant folding computes constant expressions at compile time, so they don't need calculating at run time.

questions.q: Liveness is a ___ analysis
questions.why: Liveness is a backward analysis, since it asks whether a value will be used in the future.

questions.q: Replacing i * 4 with repeated addition is
questions.why: Replacing a multiplication with repeated addition is strength reduction, which swaps an expensive operation for a cheaper one.

questions.q: Available expressions use
questions.why: Available-expressions analysis uses intersection, since the expression must be available on all incoming paths.

questions.q: Redundant MOV a, R0 after MOV R0, a is removed by
questions.why: A peephole optimiser spots local patterns like a store that immediately follows a load of the same value and removes the redundant instruction.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Loop-invariant code motion can improve performance a lot. Reason (R): Code inside loops executes many times. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: moving invariant code out of a loop can help a lot. R is true and explains it: code inside a loop runs many times, so doing it once saves repeated work.

questions.q: Leaders in: 1: x = 0; 2: L: x = x + 1; 3: if x < 10 goto L; 4: y = x
questions.why: Leaders are the first instruction (1), the target of a jump (2, label L), and the instruction after a jump (4). So the leaders are 1, 2 and 4.

questions.q: Block a = b + c; b = a + d; e = b + c (live out: e). Live on entry
questions.why: Backward: {e} → e = b + c: {b, c} → b = a + d: kills b, uses a, d → {a, c, d} → a = b + c: kills a, uses b, c → {b, c, d}.

questions.q: Case: a hot loop computes len(s) every iteration though s never changes. The compiler's fix
questions.why: Computing len(s) in every iteration when s doesn't change is loop-invariant. Loop-invariant code motion hoists it out of the loop.

questions.q: Interference graph is a cycle of 5 variables (a–b–c–d–e–a). Registers needed
questions.why: A cycle of 5 vertices is an odd cycle, which can't be 2-coloured, but 3 colours are enough. So 3 registers are needed.

questions.q: Block: t1 = a + b; t2 = a + b; t3 = t1 * t2; after CSE and copy propagation
options: t1 = a + b; t3 = t1 * t1
questions.why: t2 = a + b is the same as t1, so it's replaced by t1. Then t3 = t1 * t1. So: t1 = a + b; t3 = t1 * t1.

questions.q: How many basic blocks: 1 i = 0; 2 if i >= n goto 7; 3 s = s + i; 4 i = i + 1; 5 goto 2; 6 print 0; 7 print s
questions.why: Leaders 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 → blocks {1}, {2}, {3–5}, {6}, {7}; block {6} is unreachable.

questions.q: Sethi–Ullman: minimum registers for (a + b) * (c + d) when right leaves may be memory operands
questions.why: Each subtree (a + b and c + d) needs 1 register, and since both labels are equal, the parent needs 1 + 1 = 2 registers.

questions.q: Reaching definitions: d1 x = 1 in B1, d2 x = 2 in B2, B1 → B2 → B3 (straight line). IN[B3] for x
questions.why: d2 redefines x after d1 along the straight path, so d2 kills d1. Only d2 reaches B3, so IN[B3] = {d2}.

questions.q: Peephole: which is NOT a peephole optimisation?
questions.why: Global register allocation works across the whole function, so it isn't a peephole (local) optimisation. The other three are local patterns.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Compiler Design
courses.summary: Compiler design summary sheet, a mixed drill (FIRST/FOLLOW, LR states, TAC, scoping, liveness) and two mock papers.
outcomes: Learners can recall every compiler-design rule and formula
Learners can solve mixed GATE-style compiler questions
Learners can avoid frequent traps

scenes.text: Arjun compresses seven units into a page.
Phases, parsers, attributes, IR, runtime, optimisation.

steps.title: Front end
steps.body:
- Phases: lex → parse → semantic → ICG → optimise → codegen; symbol table everywhere
- Lex: longest match, then earlier rule
- Left recursion: A → Aα | β ⇒ A → βA', A' → αA' | ε
- FIRST/FOLLOW rules; $ ∈ FOLLOW(S); ε never in FOLLOW
- LL(1): disjoint FIRSTs; ε-alternative vs FOLLOW

steps.title: LR family
steps.body:
- LR(0) ⊂ SLR ⊂ LALR ⊂ CLR
- SLR reduces on FOLLOW; LR(1) on item lookahead
- LALR states = LR(0) states; merging may add R/R only
- YACC = LALR(1), prefers shift, %left/%right later = higher

steps.title: Translation and IR
steps.body:
- S-attributed ⊂ L-attributed
- Postfix SDT: actions at the end
- Quadruples (4 fields), triples (positions), indirect triples (pointer list), SSA (φ)
- Row-major addr = base + (i·n₂ + j)·w
- Backpatch: || patches B₁.falselist; && patches B₁.truelist

steps.title: Runtime and back end
steps.body:
- Control link = caller; access link = lexical parent
- Value / reference / value-result / name
- RC can't free cycles; copying GC compacts
- Leaders: first, jump targets, after jumps
- Liveness backward ∪; reaching defs forward ∪; available exprs forward ∩
- Registers = chromatic number of the interference graph

steps.title: Top traps
steps.body:
- Counting a string literal as many tokens
- ε-productions under FIRST instead of FOLLOW
- Thinking LALR can create new S/R conflicts
- Static vs dynamic scoping outputs
- Value-result copy-back order

quiz.why: An SLR parser reduces by A → α only when the next token is in FOLLOW(A).
Liveness analysis runs backward through the flow graph, from uses toward earlier points.
When two Lex rules match the same length, the earlier rule in the specification wins.
LALR merges LR(1) states with the same core, so it has fewer states than or the same number as canonical LR.
A copying collector moves live objects together into the other semi-space, so it compacts memory.

scenes.text: One problem per unit, three minutes each.
Compare with the worked answers.

steps.title: Drill 1 · Tokens
steps.body: `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i];` → for ( i = 0 ; i < n ; i ++ ) sum += a [ i ] ; → **20 tokens** (++ and += are single tokens).

steps.title: Drill 2 · FIRST/FOLLOW
steps.body:
S → aBDh; B → cC; C → bC | ε; D → EF; E → g | ε; F → f | ε.
FIRST(D) = {g, f, ε}; FOLLOW(D) = {h}; FOLLOW(C) = FOLLOW(B) = FIRST(D) − ε ∪ {h} = {g, f, h}.

steps.title: Drill 3 · LR
steps.body: S → CC, C → cC | d: LR(0)/SLR/LALR 7 states, CLR 10 states; grammar is LL(1) too.

steps.title: Drill 5 · Scoping
steps.body: int n = 1; void p() { n = n * 10; } void q() { int n = 2; p(); print(n); } main: q(); print(n). Static: 2 then 10. Dynamic: 20 then 1.

steps.title: Drill 6 · Liveness
steps.body: a = b + 1; c = a + b; b = c * 2 (live out: b) → live in {b}.

activity.prompt: Count tokens in the C statement given on input (same rules as Unit 1: identifiers, numbers, string literals, multi-character operators ==, !=, <=, >=, &&, ||, ++, --, +=, -=, and single characters).
activity.starter:
import re
line = input()

tests.stdin: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i];

activity.solution:
import re
line = input()
pat = r'"[^"]*"|[A-Za-z_]\w*|\d+|\+\+|--|\+=|-=|==|!=|<=|>=|&&|\|\||\S'
print(len(re.findall(pat, line)))
activity.hint: Add ++, --, += and -= before the single-character catch-all.

quiz.why: Count each lexeme (identifiers, keywords, numbers, operators and punctuation) in the drill's code. The total comes to 20 tokens.
FOLLOW(C) collects what can come after C: via B and the nullable D, it includes g, f and h. So {g, f, h}.
The element's offset is its index (219) times the element size (4): 219 × 4 = 876.
Under dynamic scoping p's n refers to the most recent binding on the stack, which is q's n. So p changes q's n to 20 and prints 20, while the global stays 1.
Working backward from the end of the block, only b is live on entry (a is redefined before use and c is defined before use). So live-in is {b}.

scenes.text: Paper A (concepts) and Paper B (problems) make the exam.
Target 45 minutes.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
- Write FIRST/FOLLOW tables neatly before filling LL(1) tables.
- For LR questions, build I0 carefully — most errors start there.
- For scoping/parameter questions, draw the stack frames.

steps.title: Mark-losing habits
steps.body:
- Missing $ in FOLLOW(S)
- Forgetting closure after goto
- Running liveness forwards
- Miscounting multi-character operators as two tokens

steps.title: Beyond the exam
steps.body: LLVM/Clang (SSA IR, passes), GCC, JIT compilers in browsers and the JVM, Python's bytecode compiler — the ideas here run all of them.

activity.prompt: I can…
items: Remove left recursion and compute FIRST/FOLLOW
Find basic blocks, liveness and registers

quiz.q: First thing to build in an LR question
quiz.why: In an LR construction question, start with the initial state I0, taking the closure of the augmented start item.
Stack-frame diagrams show the binding in each activation, which makes scoping questions much easier.
LLVM IR is in SSA form: each variable is assigned exactly once.
If $ is missing from FOLLOW(S), the ε-entries under the end-of-input column of the LL table are missed, breaking the parser.
A just-in-time (JIT) compiler compiles code at run time, while the program is executing.

questions.q: [Paper A] Lexer output
questions.why: The lexer's output is a stream of tokens, which goes to the parser.

questions.q: [Paper A] YACC produces
questions.why: YACC generates LALR parsers.

questions.q: [Paper A] Triples have
questions.why: A triple has three fields: operator, argument 1 and argument 2. The result is identified by position.

questions.q: [Paper A] Left recursion is a problem for
questions.why: Left recursion causes infinite recursion in top-down parsers, so it must be removed first.

questions.q: [Paper A] Access link supports
questions.why: Access links (the static chain) support static scoping by letting a procedure reach non-local variables.

questions.q: [Paper A] Available expressions meet
questions.why: Available expressions use intersection, because the expression must be available along every incoming path.

questions.q: [Paper A] Assertion (A): Every S-attributed SDD can be evaluated during LR parsing. Reason (R): Synthesized attributes can be computed at reductions. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: an S-attributed SDD can be evaluated during LR parsing. R is true and explains it: synthesised attributes depend only on children, so they can be computed each time the parser reduces a production.

questions.q: [Paper A] LALR merging may cause
questions.why: Merging same-core LR(1) states in LALR can combine lookahead sets in a way that makes two reductions conflict, giving reduce/reduce conflicts. It can't create new shift/reduce conflicts.

questions.q: [Paper A] Reference counting fails on
questions.why: Reference counting can't reclaim cyclic garbage: objects that refer to each other keep their counts above zero even when nothing else can reach them.

questions.q: [Paper A] Jump-to-jump elimination is a ___ optimisation
questions.why: Jump-to-jump elimination looks at a small window of instructions, so it's a peephole (local) optimisation.

questions.q: [Paper B] Tokens in `a[i] = b * 2 + c;`
questions.why: The tokens are a, [, i, ], =, b, *, 2, +, c and ;, which makes 11.

questions.q: [Paper B] FIRST(S) for S → ABc; A → a | ε; B → b | ε
questions.why: Both A and B can vanish, so FIRST(S) includes what A starts with (a), what B starts with (b) and, if both disappear, c. So {a, b, c}.

questions.q: [Paper B] Postfix of a * (b + c) − d
questions.why: The parentheses make b + c happen first: abc+. Then multiply by a: abc+*. Then subtract d: abc+*d−.

questions.q: [Paper B] int A[8][16], w = 2, base 100, row-major: A[3][4]
questions.why: Row-major address = base + (row × columns + col) × width = 100 + (3 × 16 + 4) × 2 = 100 + 52 × 2 = 204.

questions.q: [Paper B] f(x, y) { x = x * 2; y = y + x; } a = 3; f(a, a); print a — call by reference
questions.why: With call by reference, x and y both alias a. x = x × 2 makes a = 6. Then y = y + x = 6 + 6 = 12, so a is 12.

questions.q: [Paper B] Same call by value
questions.why: With call by value, f only changes its own copies, so a keeps the value 3.

questions.q: [Paper B] Interference graph K₃ plus an isolated node: registers
questions.why: K₃ is a triangle with all three nodes mutually interfering, so it needs 3 colours. The isolated node can reuse one. So 3 registers.

questions.q: [Paper B] Live-in for: x = a + b; y = x * c; a = y − 1 (live out: a, x)
questions.why: Backward: {a, x} → a = y − 1: {x, y} → y = x * c: {x, c} → x = a + b: {a, b, c}.

questions.q: [Paper B] LR(1) but not LALR(1) grammar characteristic
options: merging same-core states creates a reduce/reduce conflict
questions.why: A grammar that is LR(1) but not LALR(1) has same-core states that, when merged, produce a reduce/reduce conflict. It isn't ambiguous or left-recursive because of that.

questions.q: [Paper B] Basic blocks: 1 x = 1; 2 y = 2; 3 if x > y goto 6; 4 z = x; 5 goto 7; 6 z = y; 7 print z
questions.why: The leaders are 1 (first), 4 (after the jump in 3), 6 (a jump target) and 7 (a jump target). That gives 4 basic blocks.

steps.title: Anatomy of a program

- `using System;` imports the namespace holding `Console`.
- A `class` holds methods; `static void Main()` is the entry point.
- Statements end with `;`, blocks use `{ }`.

Since C# 9 you may also write **top-level statements** with no class at all.

Build and run

- `dotnet new console -n Hello` creates a project.
- `dotnet run` compiles to IL and runs it on the CLR.
- `Console.WriteLine` adds a newline; `Console.Write` does not.

- C# is case-sensitive: `console.writeline` fails.
- Forgetting `;`.
- `Main` must be capitalised.

quiz.q: Entry point of a C# console program
quiz.why: A C# console program starts running at the Main method, which is declared static void Main().
Console.WriteLine prints the text and then moves to a new line. Console.Write prints without the newline.
The C# compiler produces IL (Intermediate Language), which the CLR's JIT compiler turns into machine code at run time.
C# is case-sensitive, so Name and name are different identifiers.

Switching to decimal keeps ₹45.50 exact.

steps.title: Value types
steps.body:
- `int` (32-bit), `long` (64-bit), `double` (64-bit float), `decimal` (128-bit, exact for money), `bool`, `char`.
- `string` is a reference type but immutable.

steps.title: var and const
steps.body:
`var x = 5;` — type inferred at compile time (still strongly typed).
`const double Pi = 3.14159;` — compile-time constant.

steps.title: Solved example: money
Common mistakes

- `decimal d = 4.5;` fails — needs `4.5m`.
- `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is false for double.
- `var x;` without initialiser is an error.

Read two integers on separate lines and print `Sum= Product=

`.

quiz.why: decimal stores base-10 numbers exactly, which suits money. double and float are binary and can give small rounding errors.
var asks the compiler to work out the variable's type from the value on the right. It is still fixed at compile time and isn't dynamic.
A decimal literal uses the suffix m (or M), as in 4.5m. f is for float and d for double.
A string in C# is a reference type that is immutable: its content can't be changed once made.

scenes.text: Kiran's average shows 7 instead of 7.5.

steps.title: Operators

Arithmetic `+ - * / %`, comparison `== != < >`, logical `&& || !`, compound `+= ++`.
Integer `/` truncates: `15/2 == 7`.

steps.title: Conversion
steps.body:
- Implicit widening: `int → long → double`.
- Explicit cast: `(int)7.9 == 7`.
- `int.Parse(s)` throws on bad input; `int.TryParse(s, out int n)` returns bool.
- `Convert.ToInt32(s)`.

```
Console.WriteLine($"Avg={avg:F2}"); // Avg=7.50
```

activity.prompt: Read three integer marks (one per line) and print the average with 2 decimals as `Avg=<x>`.
activity.hint: Divide by 3.0, format with :F2.

quiz.why: Both operands are ints, so C# does integer division and drops the fraction: 15 / 2 = 7.

quiz.q: Safe parsing that does not throw
quiz.why: int.TryParse returns false for bad input instead of throwing an exception, so it is the safe way to parse.
The format specifier F2 prints a number with 2 digits after the decimal point.
A cast to int truncates the fraction (it doesn't round), so (int)7.9 is 7.

scenes.text: The college portal must turn ' RaVi ' into 'ravi'.
Trim() and ToLower() clean it in one line.

steps.title: Useful methods
steps.body: `Length`, `ToUpper()`, `ToLower()`, `Trim()`, `Substring(i,len)`, `IndexOf`, `Contains`, `Replace`, `Split`, `string.Join`.

steps.title: Solved example: reverse
StringBuilder
steps.body: Strings are immutable; building in a loop with `+=` creates many objects. Use `System.Text.StringBuilder` for heavy concatenation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `s.ToUpper();` alone does nothing — assign the result.
- Substring index out of range throws.

activity.prompt: Read a word and print it reversed and uppercased.
activity.hint: ToCharArray + Array.Reverse.

quiz.why: Strings are immutable, so s.ToUpper() returns a new string and leaves s unchanged. You need to assign the result.
StringBuilder changes its buffer in place, so building a string piece by piece is efficient. Repeated string += creates a new string every time.
Substring(1, 3) starts at index 1 and takes 3 characters: 'e', 'l', 'l', which gives 'ell'.
The string "C#" has 2 characters, so its Length is 2.

questions.q: C# entry point method name
questions.why: The entry point of a C# program is a method called Main, with a capital M, because C# is case-sensitive.

questions.q: Type for exact money
questions.why: decimal represents base-10 values exactly, so it's the right type for money. Float and double can give rounding errors.

questions.q: `var x = 5;` type of x
questions.why: var x = 5; infers the type from the literal 5, which is an int.

questions.q: Console method that reads a line
questions.why: Console.ReadLine reads a whole line of text from the input.

questions.q: 7/2 with ints
questions.why: Both are ints, so the division is integer division and the fraction is dropped: 7/2 = 3.

questions.q: int.TryParse returns
questions.why: int.TryParse returns a bool saying whether parsing worked. The parsed value comes back in the out parameter.
F2 formats a number to 2 decimal places, so 3.14159 prints as 3.14.

questions.q: String immutability means
questions.why: Immutability means a string never changes once created. Methods like ToUpper return a new string, they don't modify the original.

questions.q: `decimal d = 4.5;` gives
questions.why: 4.5 is a double literal, and C# has no implicit conversion from double to decimal, so decimal d = 4.5; is a compile error (CS0664). Write 4.5m instead.
Casting to int truncates toward zero, so (int)−2.7 is −2, not −3.

questions.q: "abc".IndexOf('z')
questions.why: IndexOf returns −1 when the character isn't found, rather than throwing an exception.

questions.q: Best for building a 10,000-part string
questions.why: For a string made of many parts, StringBuilder is best. Using += would copy the whole string every time.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Control flow & methods

scenes.text: The exam cell needs grades from marks.
An if-else ladder maps 90+ to A, 75+ to B and so on.

steps.title: if / else if / else
steps.body: Conditions must be `bool` — `if (x)` with int x does not compile, unlike C.

steps.title: switch
steps.body:
Classic `switch` with `case` and `break` (fall-through between non-empty cases is not allowed), plus C# 8 **switch expressions**:
```
string d = n switch { 1 => "Mon", 2 => "Tue", _ => "?" };
```

steps.title: Solved example: ternary
steps.body: `string r = m >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";`

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing `break` in a non-empty case is a compile error.
- Order of conditions in a ladder matters (check 90 before 75).

activity.prompt: Read marks (0–100). Print A (>=90), B (>=75), C (>=50), else F.
activity.hint: Check the highest threshold first.

quiz.q: C# switch fall-through between non-empty cases is
quiz.why: C# doesn't allow a non-empty switch case to fall through into the next one. Each such case must end with break, return or similar.
In a switch expression, the discard _ matches anything left over, so it works as the default case.
An if condition must be a bool. Unlike C, C# doesn't accept an int such as 1 or 0.
With m = 40, the test m >= 40 is true, so the conditional operator gives the first value, "P".

scenes.text: A Class 3 teacher asks a CSE student for a times-table printer.
A for loop prints every line.

steps.title: Loop forms
steps.body:
- `for (int i=0;i<n;i++)` when count is known.
- `while (cond)` checks first.
- `do { } while (cond);` runs at least once.
- `foreach (var x in arr)` reads each element.

steps.title: break and continue
steps.body: `break` exits the loop; `continue` skips to the next iteration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Off-by-one: `i<=n` vs `i<n`.
- Modifying a collection inside foreach throws.
- Forgetting to update the while variable → infinite loop.

activity.prompt: Read n and print `n x i = r` for i from 1 to 3.
activity.hint: for i from 1 to 3 inclusive.

quiz.q: Loop that always runs at least once
quiz.why: A do-while loop tests its condition after the body, so the body always runs at least once.
continue skips the rest of the current iteration and goes on to the next one.
Digits of 405 are 4, 0 and 5, and 4 + 0 + 5 = 9.

quiz.q: Changing a List inside foreach over it
quiz.why: Changing a List while iterating over it with foreach makes its enumerator invalid, so it throws an InvalidOperationException.

scenes.text: Three screens compute GST with copy-pasted code; a bug fix is applied to only one.
A single method fixes it everywhere.

steps.title: Defining methods
steps.body:
`static int Add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`
Expression-bodied: `static int Sq(int x) => x * x;`

steps.title: Parameter passing
steps.body:
- Default: by value (a copy).
- `ref`: caller variable must be initialised; method can change it.
- `out`: method must assign it (e.g. TryParse).
- `in`: read-only reference.
- Optional `int b = 10` and named args `Add(b: 2, a: 1)`.
- Overloading: same name, different parameter lists.

steps.title: Solved example: swap
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `ref` at the call site.
- Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads.

activity.prompt: Write `static int Max3(int a,int b,int c)`. Read three ints (one per line) and print the maximum.
activity.hint: Math.Max nests nicely.

quiz.why: An out parameter must be assigned inside the method before it returns. The caller doesn't need to initialise it.
Overloaded methods share a name but differ in their parameter list (number, types or order). Return type alone isn't enough.
By default, C# passes arguments by value: the method gets a copy. Use ref or out to pass by reference.
The => after a method signature is an expression-bodied member: a short way to write a method that just returns an expression.

scenes.text: The sports day needs the top score among 200 runners.
An array plus a loop finds it; recursion computes factorial for a prize puzzle.

steps.title: Arrays
steps.body: `int[] a = new int[5];` zero-filled; `int[] b = {1,2,3};` `a.Length`. Rectangular `int[,] m = new int[3,3];` and jagged `int[][]`.

steps.title: Recursion
steps.body:
A method calling itself with a **base case**:
```
static long Fact(int n) => n <= 1 ? 1 : n * Fact(n - 1);
```

steps.title: Solved example: split input
steps.body: `int[] nums = Array.ConvertAll(Console.ReadLine().Split(' '), int.Parse);`

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Index `a[a.Length]` → IndexOutOfRangeException.
- No base case → StackOverflowException.

activity.prompt: Read n, print n! (n ≤ 20) using a recursive method.
activity.hint: Base case n <= 1 returns 1.

quiz.why: Array elements of a numeric type are set to 0 by default, so new int[3] contains 0, 0, 0.

quiz.q: Last index of array length n
quiz.why: Arrays are zero-based, so the last index of an array of length n is n − 1.
A recursive method with no base case calls itself forever, until the call stack runs out and a StackOverflowException happens.
int[,] declares a rectangular two-dimensional array, where every row has the same length. A jagged array is int[][].

questions.q: Loop that runs at least once
questions.why: A do-while loop checks its condition at the end, so the body runs at least once.

questions.q: switch fall-through in C#
questions.why: C# doesn't allow non-empty switch cases to fall through. Each one must end with break, return or goto.

questions.q: break does
questions.why: break exits the nearest enclosing loop (or switch) at once.

questions.q: Parameter the method must assign
questions.why: An out parameter must be assigned by the method before it returns.

questions.q: Overloading by return type only
questions.why: Methods can't be overloaded by return type alone, because the compiler picks the method from the arguments, not the expected return.

questions.q: int[][] is
questions.why: int[][] is a jagged array, an array of arrays whose rows can have different lengths. A rectangular array is int[,].

questions.q: Sum of digits of 999
questions.why: The digits of 999 add up to 9 + 9 + 9 = 27.

questions.q: Infinite recursion error
questions.why: Infinite recursion fills the call stack, causing a StackOverflowException.

questions.q: `params int[] a` allows
questions.why: A params parameter lets a method accept any number of arguments of that type, collected into an array.

questions.q: Swap(int a,int b) without ref
questions.why: Without ref, ints are passed by value, so the method swaps only its own copies. The caller's variables stay unchanged.

questions.q: n switch {1=>"a", _=>"b"} with n=5
questions.why: With n = 5, the pattern 1 doesn't match, so the discard _ applies and the result is "b".

questions.q: Recursive Fib(6) with Fib(0)=0, Fib(1)=1
questions.why: The Fibonacci sequence is 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, so Fib(6) = 8.

courses.title: Unit 3 · OOP in C#
courses.summary: Classes, properties, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces, structs, records and static members. Covers topics commonly taught in B.Tech CSE programmes, with runnable console programs.
outcomes: Learners can explain the key ideas of OOP in C#
Learners can write and run short C# console programs on these topics
Learners can spot and fix common mistakes

scenes.text: The department library tracks books in parallel arrays and they fall out of sync.
A Book class with properties keeps each book's data together.

steps.title: Class and object
Properties
steps.body: Auto-properties generate a hidden field. Use `get`/`set` with logic for validation; `init` (C# 9) allows set only at creation. Access modifiers: `public`, `private` (default for members), `protected`, `internal`.

steps.title: Solved example: validation
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Making fields public instead of properties.
- Using an object variable before `new` → NullReferenceException.

activity.prompt: Create class `Rect` with properties W and H and method Area(). Read W and H (lines) and print `Area=<a>`.
activity.hint: Object initialiser: new Rect { W = w, H = h }.

quiz.q: Default access of a class member
quiz.why: The default access for class members is private, so they can be seen only inside the class.
An init accessor lets a property be set only while the object is being created (in a constructor or object initialiser), then it's read-only.
An auto-property such as public int X { get; set; } makes the compiler create a hidden backing field for you.

quiz.q: Calling a method on a null reference
quiz.why: Using a member on a null reference throws a NullReferenceException at run time.

scenes.text: Interns, employees and managers all get paid differently.
A base Employee with virtual Pay() lets each subclass override it.

steps.title: Inheritance
steps.body: `class Manager : Employee` — single class inheritance only. `base(...)` calls the parent constructor. `sealed` prevents inheritance.

steps.title: virtual / override / abstract
steps.body:
- `virtual` method can be overridden with `override`.
- `abstract` class cannot be instantiated; abstract methods have no body.
- `new` hides (not overrides) — calls through a base reference use the base version.

steps.title: Solved example
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `virtual` in base → can't override.
- Confusing `new` with `override`.

activity.prompt: Base `Animal` with virtual Speak() returning "...". `Dog` returns "Woof", `Cat` returns "Meow". Read dog or cat and print Speak() via an Animal reference.
activity.hint: Mark the base method virtual, subclasses override.

quiz.why: C# classes allow single inheritance: one base class only. They can implement many interfaces.
A sealed class can't be used as a base class, so nothing can inherit from it.
An abstract class is incomplete by design, so you can't create an instance of it directly. You create objects of its concrete subclasses.
The base keyword refers to the parent class, so base(...) in a constructor initialiser calls the parent constructor.

scenes.text: The fee portal accepts UPI, card and net banking.
An IPayment interface lets new methods plug in without touching checkout code.

steps.title: Interfaces
steps.body: `interface IPayment { bool Pay(decimal amt); }` A class can implement many interfaces. Since C# 8 interfaces may have default implementations.

steps.title: struct vs class
steps.body:
- `struct`: value type, copied on assignment, no inheritance (can implement interfaces). Good for small data like points.
- `class`: reference type.

steps.title: records
steps.body: `record Point(int X, int Y);` — immutable by default, value-based equality, `with` expressions: `p with { X = 5 }`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting struct changes through a copy to affect the original.
- Comparing classes with `==` expecting value equality.

activity.prompt: Define `record Point(int X, int Y)`. Read four ints (lines) x1 y1 x2 y2 and print True if the points are equal, else False.
activity.hint: Records compare by value.

quiz.why: A C# class can implement as many interfaces as it needs.
A struct is a value type: assigning it copies the data. A class is a reference type.
Records give value-based equality: two records are equal when their property values are equal, not only when they're the same object.
The with expression on a record makes a copy of it with the listed properties changed, leaving the original unchanged.

lessons.title: Static members, encapsulation and SOLID basics

scenes.text: Each new ticket must get the next number, shared across all counters.
A static counter field belongs to the class, not to each object.

steps.title: static
steps.body: Static fields/methods belong to the type. `static class` (like `Math`) cannot be instantiated. A static constructor runs once before first use.

steps.title: Encapsulation
steps.body: Keep fields private, expose behaviour. Prefer `private set` or readonly fields.

steps.title: SOLID in one line each
steps.body:
- **S**ingle responsibility
- **O**pen/closed
- **L**iskov substitution
- **I**nterface segregation
- **D**ependency inversion (depend on interfaces; .NET has built-in dependency injection).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using static mutable state everywhere — hard to test.
- Accessing instance members from a static method without an object.

activity.prompt: Class `Ticket` has a static counter; each new Ticket gets Id = ++counter. Read n, create n tickets, print the last Id.
activity.hint: static int counter shared by all.

quiz.why: A static field belongs to the class itself, so all instances share one copy.
Math is a static class: it can't be instantiated and holds only static members like Math.Sqrt.
The D in SOLID is the dependency inversion principle: depend on abstractions (interfaces), not on concrete classes.

quiz.q: Static method using an instance field directly
quiz.why: A static method has no instance, so using an instance field directly in it is a compile error.

questions.q: Default member access
questions.why: If you don't state an access modifier, class members are private by default.

questions.q: Keyword to call parent constructor
questions.why: The base keyword refers to the parent class and is used to call its constructor.

questions.q: Abstract class can be instantiated
questions.why: An abstract class can't be instantiated. Only a concrete derived class can be.

questions.q: struct is a
questions.why: A struct is a value type, copied on assignment, while a class is a reference type.

questions.q: Multiple interfaces per class
questions.why: C# allows a class to implement several interfaces, though only one base class.

questions.q: Records give
questions.why: Records are designed for value equality: they compare their contents, not references.

questions.q: Overriding requires the base method to be
questions.why: You can only override a base method that is declared virtual, abstract or override itself.

questions.q: `new` modifier on a method
questions.why: The new modifier on a method hides the base class member of the same name. It doesn't override it.

questions.q: Static constructor runs
questions.why: A static constructor runs once, automatically, before the class is first used. It isn't called for each object.

questions.q: Base reference calling a `new`-hidden method calls
questions.why: A method hidden with new is chosen by the variable's declared type. A base-type reference therefore calls the base version.

questions.q: Modifying a copied struct
questions.why: A struct is copied by value, so changing the copy leaves the original unchanged.

questions.q: Liskov substitution says
options: subtypes must be usable wherever the base type is
questions.why: The Liskov substitution principle says that objects of a subclass must be usable wherever the base class is expected without breaking the program.

Learners can write and run short C# console programs on these topics
Learners can spot and fix common mistakes

scenes.text: Ma'am wants roll numbers mapped to names.
Dictionary<int,string> gives fast lookup.

steps.title: Generic collections
steps.body:
In System.Collections.Generic:
- `List<T>`: resizable array, `Add`, `Remove`, `Count`, index.
- `Dictionary<K,V>`: hash map, `TryGetValue`, `ContainsKey`.
- `HashSet<T>`: unique items.
- `Queue<T>` FIFO, `Stack<T>` LIFO.

steps.title: Solved example: word count
Complexity
steps.body: List index O(1), add at end amortised O(1); Dictionary lookup average O(1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `d[key]` for a missing key throws KeyNotFoundException.
- Mixing `Count()` (LINQ) with the `Count` property.

activity.prompt: Read a line of space-separated words and print the number of distinct words.
activity.hint: A HashSet keeps unique items.

quiz.why: Queue<T> is first-in, first-out (FIFO): items leave in the order they arrived. Stack<T> is last-in, first-out.
Reading d[key] for a key that doesn't exist throws a KeyNotFoundException. Use TryGetValue to avoid it.
A Dictionary uses hashing, so a lookup takes O(1) time on average.
A HashSet<T> holds each value at most once, so it keeps only unique items.

scenes.text: Rohan writes IntBox, StringBox and DoubleBox classes.
A single Box<T> replaces all three, type-safely.

steps.title: Generic types and methods
Constraints
steps.body: `where T : class`, `struct`, `new()`, a base class, or an interface.

steps.title: Why generics
steps.body: No boxing for value types and compile-time type safety, unlike the old `ArrayList` of `object`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Using `<` on T without a constraint is not allowed; use IComparable<T>.

activity.prompt: Write generic `static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>`. Read two words and print the larger (string order), then two ints and print the larger.
activity.hint: Use CompareTo.

quiz.why: Generics keep the type known at compile time, so there's no boxing of value types and no casting is needed.
The constraint where T : new() requires T to have a public parameterless constructor, so the code can write new T().
To compare values of type T with CompareTo, T must be constrained to IComparable<T>, so the compiler knows it can be compared.
List<T> is a generic collection. The non-generic ArrayList stores objects.

scenes.text: When results publish, SMS, email and app notifications must all fire.
An event lets each notifier subscribe.

steps.title: Delegates
steps.body: Type-safe references to methods. Built-ins: `Func<int,int>` (returns a value), `Action<string>` (void), `Predicate<T>`.

steps.title: Lambdas
steps.body: `Func<int,int> sq = x => x * x;` Lambdas can capture outer variables (closures).

steps.title: Events
steps.body: `public event Action<string> Published;` subscribers use `+=`; raise with `Published?.Invoke(msg);`

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Raising an event with no subscribers without `?.` → NullReferenceException.
- Forgetting to unsubscribe (memory leaks).

activity.prompt: Read n. Using `Func<int,int> sq = x => x*x;` print sq(n), then use an `Action<int>` to print `Done <n>`.
activity.hint: Func returns a value; Action doesn't.

quiz.q: Delegate for a void method taking string
quiz.why: Action<string> is a delegate for a method that takes a string and returns void. Func delegates return a value.

quiz.q: In Func<int,int> the last type parameter is
quiz.why: In Func<int,int>, the last type parameter is the return type, and the ones before it are the argument types.
Published?.Invoke(x) raises the event only if there are subscribers, so there's no NullReferenceException.
A lambda that uses variables from the surrounding method captures them. Such a lambda is called a closure.

scenes.text: The HOD wants the top 3 students with CGPA above 8, sorted.
One LINQ query: Where, OrderByDescending, Take.

steps.title: LINQ operators
steps.body: `Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy/ThenBy`, `GroupBy`, `Sum`, `Average`, `Count`, `Any`, `All`, `First/FirstOrDefault`, `Take`, `Skip`, `Distinct`. Needs `using System.Linq;`.

steps.title: Deferred execution
steps.body: Queries run only when enumerated (`foreach`, `ToList()`, `Count()`). Aggregates and `ToList` execute immediately.

steps.title: Solved example
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `First()` on an empty sequence throws; use `FirstOrDefault()`.
- Re-enumerating an expensive query many times.

activity.prompt: Read space-separated integers. Using LINQ print the sum of the squares of the even numbers.
activity.hint: Where → Select → Sum.

quiz.why: LINQ queries use deferred execution: they run only when you enumerate the results (for example with foreach or ToList).
First() throws an InvalidOperationException when the sequence is empty. FirstOrDefault returns the default value instead.
Select projects (transforms) each element into a new form. Where filters, Take limits and Any tests.
The LINQ methods are in the System.Linq namespace, so you add using System.Linq;.

questions.q: LIFO collection
questions.why: Stack<T> is last-in, first-out (LIFO): the most recently pushed item is popped first.

questions.q: Missing key in d[key]
questions.why: Reading a key that isn't in the dictionary with d[key] throws a KeyNotFoundException.

questions.q: Namespace for LINQ
questions.why: LINQ lives in the System.Linq namespace.

questions.q: Func<int,string> returns
questions.why: In Func<int,string> the last type parameter is the return type, so it returns a string.

questions.q: Lambda x => x*2 applied to 4
questions.why: The lambda x => x * 2 doubles its argument, so for 4 it gives 8.

questions.q: Where does
questions.why: Where filters a sequence, keeping only the elements that satisfy a condition.

questions.q: LINQ execution by default
questions.why: LINQ queries are deferred by default: they execute when the results are enumerated, not when the query is written.

questions.q: Constraint for a parameterless constructor
questions.why: The new() constraint requires the type to have a public parameterless constructor.

questions.q: Safe event invocation
questions.why: E?.Invoke() raises the event only if someone has subscribed (E isn't null), which is the safe pattern.
Where(x > 2) keeps 3 and 4, and their Sum is 3 + 4 = 7.

questions.q: First() on an empty sequence
questions.why: First() throws an InvalidOperationException on an empty sequence, since there is no first element.

questions.q: Main benefit of List<int> over ArrayList
questions.why: List<int> is generic: it stores ints directly with no boxing and checks types at compile time. ArrayList holds objects and needs casts.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Exceptions, files, async & .NET overview
