story.title: Finding a book in a library

scenes.text: A library with 1 lakh books: scanning every shelf is slow; a catalogue card points straight to the shelf.
Indexes are a database's catalogue.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
- **Blocking factor** bfr = ⌊block size / record size⌋ records per block (unspanned). Blocks b = ⌈r / bfr⌉.
- **Heap file:** linear search ≈ b/2 block reads on average (b worst). **Sorted file:** binary search ⌈log₂ b⌉.
- **Primary index:** on the ordering key of a sorted file; **sparse** (one entry per block).
- **Clustering index:** on a non-key ordering field.
- **Secondary index:** on a non-ordering field; **dense** (one entry per record).
- **Multilevel index:** index on the index; fan-out fo = ⌊block / entry⌋; levels ≈ ⌈log_fo(entries)⌉.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Binary search vs primary index
steps.body:
r = 30,000 records, record 100 B, block 1024 B → bfr = 10 → b = 3000 blocks.
- Binary search: ⌈log₂ 3000⌉ = **12** block reads.
- Primary index: entry = key 9 B + pointer 6 B = 15 B → 68 entries/block; 3000 entries → ⌈3000/68⌉ = 45 index blocks → ⌈log₂ 45⌉ = 6, + 1 data block = **7** reads.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Multilevel index
steps.body: Same index with fan-out 68: level 1 has 45 blocks; level 2 needs ⌈45/68⌉ = 1 block. Levels = 2 → access = 2 + 1 = **3** block reads.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rounding bfr up (it must be floored for unspanned records).
- Forgetting the final data-block access.
- Saying a secondary index can be sparse — it must be dense (file not ordered on that field).

activity.prompt: 1,00,000 records of 200 B in 4096 B blocks (unspanned). How many blocks does the file need?

quiz.q: Sparse index has one entry per
quiz.why: A sparse index has one entry per block (not per record), and it requires the file to be sorted on the indexed key.
A secondary index is on a field that the file isn't sorted by, so it must have an entry for every record: it's dense.

quiz.q: Binary search on 1024 blocks needs about
quiz.why: Binary search halves the range each time, so 1024 = 2¹⁰ blocks need about 10 block reads.

quiz.q: bfr for 512 B blocks and 100 B records
quiz.why: The blocking factor is ⌊512/100⌋ = 5 records per block. We take the floor since a record can't be split across blocks here.

quiz.q: A file can have how many primary (ordering-key) indexes?
quiz.why: A file can be physically ordered in only one way, so it has at most one primary (ordering-key) index.

scenes.text: Every insert and delete keeps all leaves at the same depth.
That's why almost every relational database uses B+ trees for indexes.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
**B-tree of order p:** each node has ≤ p children and ≤ p − 1 keys; non-root internal nodes ≥ ⌈p/2⌉ children; keys and data pointers in all nodes.
**B+ tree:** internal nodes hold only keys + child pointers (higher fan-out); **all record pointers are in the leaves**, which are linked for range scans. Every search goes to a leaf (height + 1 node reads). Insertion splits overflowing nodes and pushes a key up; deletion merges/redistributes.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Order of nodes
steps.body:
Block 512 B, key 10 B, block pointer 6 B, record pointer 7 B.
- **Internal** (p pointers, p − 1 keys): 6p + 10(p − 1) ≤ 512 → 16p ≤ 522 → **p = 32**.
- **Leaf** (q key–record-pointer pairs + 1 next pointer): 17q + 6 ≤ 512 → **q = 29**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Height for 1 million keys
steps.body: Internal fan-out 32 (assume ~full), leaves hold 29 keys. Leaves needed ≈ ⌈10⁶ / 29⌉ = 34,483. Internal levels: 32 → 32² = 1024 → 32³ = 32,768 (< 34,483) → 32⁴ — so **4 internal levels + leaf level**: about 5 node reads, + 1 for the record = 6. Real trees are ~69% full, giving one more level at most.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Insert with split
steps.body: B+ tree, leaf capacity 3 keys. Leaf [10, 20, 30] receives 25 → [10, 20, 25, 30] overflows → split into [10, 20] and [25, 30]; copy **25** up into the parent (in a B+ tree the separator stays in the leaf; in a B-tree the middle key moves up).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the record-pointer size for internal nodes of a B+ tree (they have block pointers only).
- Forgetting the p − 1 keys term.
- Thinking B+ tree internal keys must also exist as records — they are separators.

activity.prompt: Block 1024 B, key 12 B, block pointer 8 B. Order p of a B+ tree internal node (p·8 + (p−1)·12 ≤ 1024)?

quiz.q: Range queries are efficient in B+ trees because
quiz.why: B+ tree leaves are linked in key order, so a range query finds the start and then scans the leaves sequentially.

quiz.q: Record pointers in a B+ tree are stored in
quiz.why: In a B+ tree, the record (data) pointers are stored only in the leaf nodes. Internal nodes only guide the search.

quiz.q: Minimum children of a non-root internal node of order p
quiz.why: A non-root internal node must be at least half full, so it has at least ⌈p/2⌉ children.

quiz.q: Why is B+ tree fan-out higher than B-tree's?
options: no data pointers in internal nodes
quiz.why: B+ internal nodes have no data pointers, so more keys and child pointers fit in a block. That gives a higher fan-out and a shorter tree.

quiz.q: In a B+ tree split, the separator key is
quiz.why: When a B+ tree leaf splits, the separator key is copied up to the parent and also stays in the leaf. In an internal node split, the key moves up.

scenes.text: A gym assigns lockers by member ID mod 100. Finding a locker takes one step — unless two members collide.
Hashing gives O(1) equality lookups but cannot do ranges.

steps.title: Hashing
steps.body:
- **Static hashing:** h(K) mod M buckets; overflow chains when buckets fill; poor when the file grows.
- **Extendible hashing:** directory of 2^d pointers (global depth d); buckets have local depth; a full bucket splits, and the directory doubles only when local depth = global depth.
- **Linear hashing:** buckets split in a fixed round-robin order, no directory.
Hash indexes support equality, not range queries.

steps.title: Query processing
steps.body:
Parse → translate to relational algebra → optimise (equivalence rules: push σ down, push π down, reorder joins) → choose access paths and join algorithms → execute.
Join algorithms: **nested loop** (block nested loop cost ≈ b_R + b_R × b_S with one buffer block per relation), **index nested loop**, **sort–merge**, **hash join**. Use the smaller relation as the outer relation.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Extendible hashing
steps.body: Global depth 2 (directory 00, 01, 10, 11), bucket capacity 2. Bucket for 01 has local depth 2 and is full; inserting another key with suffix 01 → local depth = global depth → **directory doubles** to depth 3 (8 entries) and the bucket splits into 001 and 101.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Nested-loop cost
steps.body: b_R = 100 blocks, b_S = 400 blocks, one block buffer each. R outer: 100 + 100 × 400 = **40,100** block transfers. S outer: 400 + 400 × 100 = 40,400. With enough memory to hold R entirely: 100 + 400 = **500**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing hashing for range queries.
- Doubling the extendible-hashing directory on every split.
- Putting the larger relation as the outer loop.

activity.prompt: Block nested-loop join: b_R = 50 blocks (outer), b_S = 200 blocks, one buffer block each. Block transfers = b_R + b_R × b_S?

quiz.why: A hash index scatters keys, so it keeps no order. It's good for equality lookups, but poor for range searches.

quiz.q: Extendible hashing doubles the directory when
options: a full bucket's local depth equals global depth
quiz.why: In extendible hashing, if a full bucket's local depth equals the global depth, the directory must double before the bucket can split. Otherwise just the bucket splits.

quiz.q: Pushing selections down the query tree
quiz.why: Pushing selections down the query tree filters rows early, so intermediate results are smaller and later operations are cheaper.

quiz.q: Best outer relation for block nested-loop
quiz.why: Using the smaller relation as the outer one in block nested-loop join gives fewer outer iterations, so the inner relation is scanned fewer times.
Linear hashing grows by splitting buckets one at a time in round-robin order, with no directory.

scenes.text: Before changing any balance, the bank writes the old and new values in a diary.
After a crash, it reads the diary: redo what was committed, undo what was not.

steps.title: Logs and rules
steps.body:
Log records: <T start>, <T, X, old, new>, <T commit>, <T abort>.
- **Write-ahead logging (WAL):** the log record must reach stable storage *before* the data page is written; all log records of T are flushed before T commits.
- **Deferred modification:** writes applied only after commit → only **redo** needed.
- **Immediate modification:** writes may reach disk before commit → **undo** (uncommitted, in reverse order) and **redo** (committed, in forward order).
- **Checkpoint:** flush log and dirty pages, write <checkpoint L> (L = active transactions); recovery starts scanning from the last checkpoint.
- **ARIES** (used by many systems): analysis, redo (repeat history), undo phases with LSNs and compensation log records.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Recover after crash
steps.body:
Log: <T1 start> <T1, A, 100, 50> <T2 start> <T2, B, 200, 250> <T1 commit> <T3 start> <T3, C, 10, 20> — crash.
- Committed: T1 → **redo** A = 50.
- Uncommitted: T2, T3 → **undo** C = 10, B = 200 (reverse order).
- Final: A = 50, B = 200, C = 10.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · With a checkpoint
steps.body:
… <T1 commit> <checkpoint {T2}> <T2, B, 250, 300> <T4 start> <T4, D, 1, 2> <T4 commit> — crash.
- T1 committed before the checkpoint → nothing to do.
- T4 committed after → **redo** D = 2.
- T2 still active → **undo** all its changes (including those before the checkpoint).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Undoing in forward order (must be reverse).
- Ignoring transactions that were active at the checkpoint.
- Thinking deferred modification ever needs undo.

activity.prompt: Order the recovery steps for immediate modification after a crash
items: Build lists of committed and uncommitted transactions
Undo uncommitted transactions scanning the log backward
Redo committed transactions scanning the log forward
Write <T abort> records for undone transactions

quiz.q: WAL requires the log record be written
quiz.why: Write-ahead logging requires the log record for a change to be written to stable storage before the changed data page is written.
With deferred modification, changes reach the database only after commit, so nothing uncommitted is on disk, and recovery needs only redo.

quiz.q: Uncommitted transactions after a crash are
quiz.why: After a crash, transactions that hadn't committed are undone (rolled back) so the database stays consistent.
A checkpoint records a consistent point, so recovery needs to scan only the log after it, which shortens both the log and the recovery time.
ARIES recovery has three phases: analysis, redo and undo.

questions.q: Dense index has an entry for every
questions.why: A dense index has an entry for every record.

questions.q: B+ tree leaves are
questions.why: B+ tree leaves are linked in order, which supports efficient range scans and sequential access.

questions.q: WAL stands for
questions.why: WAL stands for write-ahead logging: the log is written before the data.

questions.q: Binary search on 4096 blocks costs
questions.why: 4096 = 2¹², so binary search needs about 12 block reads.

questions.q: Which supports range queries best?
questions.why: A B+ tree keeps keys in sorted, linked leaves, so range queries are efficient. Hash indexes can't do ranges.

questions.q: Immediate modification recovery needs
questions.why: With immediate modification, changes may reach disk before commit, so recovery needs undo for uncommitted ones and redo for committed ones not yet written.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A file can have many secondary indexes. Reason (R): A secondary index does not depend on the file's physical order. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: a file can have many secondary indexes. R is true and explains it: a secondary index doesn't depend on the file's physical order, so you can build one on each field.

questions.q: Block 2048 B, record 150 B: bfr
Block nested-loop: b_R = 20 (outer), b_S = 1000: transfers
questions.why: Block nested loop with outer R: read R once (20 blocks) and S once per outer block: 20 × 1000 = 20,000. Total = 20 + 20,000 = 20,020.

questions.q: Case: a reporting query filters `WHERE amount BETWEEN 1000 AND 5000` on 50 million rows. Best index?
questions.why: A range condition (BETWEEN) is best served by a B+ tree on amount, since its leaves are in order. A hash index can't do ranges.

questions.q: B+ tree: block 1024 B, key 9 B, block pointer 7 B. Internal order p:
questions.why: An internal node holds p pointers and p − 1 keys: 7p + 9(p − 1) ≤ 1024 → 16p ≤ 1033 → p = 64.

questions.q: Same, leaf with record pointer 7 B and one next pointer 7 B: q
questions.why: A leaf holds q (key + record pointer) pairs plus one next pointer: q(9 + 7) + 7 ≤ 1024 → 16q ≤ 1017 → q = 63.

questions.q: Log: <T1 start> <T1, A, 5, 10> <T1 commit> <T2 start> <T2, A, 10, 20> — crash. Value of A after recovery (immediate modification)?
questions.why: Redo committed T1 (A = 10), undo uncommitted T2 (restore old value 10) → A = 10.

questions.q: r = 2,00,000 records, 10 per block, primary index fan-out 100. Multilevel index access cost (levels + 1 data block)
questions.why: 20,000 blocks → index L1 200 blocks → L2 2 blocks → L3 1 block: 3 levels + 1 = 4.

questions.q: Extendible hashing with global depth 3 has how many directory entries?
questions.why: The directory in extendible hashing has 2^(global depth) entries: 2³ = 8.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: A checkpoint shortens the recovery scan. Deferred modification needs redo only, a sparse index needs sorted data, and hashing doesn't support range queries.

scenes.text: Sana prints one page of DBMS rules the night before her exam.
Each rule comes with its trap.

steps.title: Modelling and algebra
steps.body:
- 1:N → FK on N side; M:N → new table; multivalued → new table; weak → owner PK + partial key
- Superkeys with single key A in n attributes: 2ⁿ⁻¹
- |R × S| = |R||S|; natural join with no common attributes = product
- R ÷ S = π_A(R) − π_A((π_A(R) × S) − R)

steps.title: SQL
steps.body:
- Order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
- Aggregates ignore NULL (except COUNT(*)); NOT IN with NULL → empty
- Second highest: MAX(salary) WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX…)
- RANK leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK does not

steps.title: Normalization
steps.body:
- Attributes never on RHS ∈ every key
- 2NF: no partial; 3NF: X superkey or A prime; BCNF: X superkey
- Lossless: (R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or R2
- 3NF synthesis: lossless + dependency preserving; BCNF: lossless only

steps.title: Transactions and storage
steps.body:
- Conflict serializable ⇔ acyclic precedence graph
- Recoverable: writer commits before reader commits; cascadeless: no dirty reads
- 2PL ⇒ conflict serializable; not deadlock-free
- Wait–die: older waits, younger dies; wound–wait: older wounds, younger waits
- B+ internal: p·P + (p − 1)K ≤ B; leaf: q(K + Pr) + P ≤ B
- Recovery: undo uncommitted (backward), redo committed (forward)

steps.title: Top traps
steps.body:
- Superkey ≠ candidate key (check minimality)
- WHERE cannot use aggregates — use HAVING
- View-serializable does not imply conflict-serializable
- Floor the blocking factor
- NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns nothing

cards.back: X → A: X superkey or A prime

quiz.why: A candidate key is a minimal superkey: no attribute can be removed without losing the uniqueness property.
HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.

options: common attrs as key of one side
quiz.why: A binary decomposition is lossless if the common attributes form a key of at least one of the two parts.
Two-phase locking can deadlock, since transactions can wait for each other's locks. Conservative 2PL avoids this.
During recovery, the redo phase scans the log forward. Undo goes backward.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: Tables: **dept(name, city)** — IT/Pune, HR/Delhi, Sales/Mumbai, Legal/Chennai. **emp(id, name, dept, salary, mgr)** — 1 Asha IT 90000 NULL · 2 Ravi IT 60000 1 · 3 Meena HR 50000 1 · 4 Kabir HR 45000 3 · 5 Zoya Sales 55000 1 · 6 Dev Sales 40000 5.

steps.body: R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → C, B → D, CD → E}. A and B never on RHS; AB⁺ = A B C D E → key **AB** only. A → C is a partial dependency → highest NF **1NF**.

steps.title: Approach
steps.body:
- For normalization: always find all candidate keys first.
- For SQL output questions: write the intermediate table on paper.
- For schedules: list conflicting pairs systematically item by item.

steps.title: Mark-losing habits
steps.body:

- Not checking minimality of keys
- Forgetting NULL semantics in WHERE and NOT IN

steps.title: Interview link
steps.body: Common interview asks: 2nd highest salary, joins vs subqueries, normalization vs denormalization trade-offs, ACID vs BASE, index choice. You now have all of them.

Write joins, subqueries and GROUP BY confidently
Find candidate keys and the highest NF

quiz.q: First step in a normalization question
quiz.why: In a normalisation question, first find the candidate keys. They tell you which attributes are prime and so which normal form holds.

quiz.q: SQL output questions are best solved by
quiz.why: For SQL output questions, write out the intermediate tables step by step (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, …) to avoid mistakes.
List the conflicting operation pairs item by item (every read/write on the same item by different transactions) to build the precedence graph systematically.
Denormalisation adds redundancy on purpose, so queries need fewer joins and read faster. The cost is extra storage and harder updates.

quiz.q: NULL = NULL in SQL evaluates to
quiz.why: Comparing NULL with NULL gives UNKNOWN, not TRUE, because SQL uses three-valued logic. Use IS NULL.

questions.q: [Paper A] M:N relationship maps to
questions.why: An M:N relationship can't be held by a foreign key on either side, so it becomes a new table.

questions.q: [Paper A] π in algebra removes
questions.why: In relational algebra, projection works on sets, so it removes duplicate rows.

questions.q: [Paper A] COUNT(*) on emp
questions.why: COUNT(*) counts all rows. The emp table has 6 rows.

questions.q: [Paper A] BCNF ⊂ ?
questions.why: BCNF is stricter than 3NF, so every BCNF relation is in 3NF: BCNF ⊂ 3NF.

questions.q: [Paper A] Strict 2PL holds X locks until
questions.why: Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until the transaction commits or aborts, to avoid cascading rollbacks.

questions.q: [Paper A] Hashing is best for
questions.why: Hashing takes O(1) time for equality lookups, but it doesn't support ranges or sorting.

questions.q: [Paper A] Assertion (A): BCNF decomposition may lose FDs. Reason (R): BCNF only guarantees lossless join. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: BCNF decomposition may lose FDs. R is true and explains it: BCNF guarantees only a lossless join, not dependency preservation.

questions.q: [Paper A] `SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept IN (SELECT name FROM dept WHERE city='Mumbai') ORDER BY name;`
questions.why: Sales is the department in Mumbai, so the subquery returns Sales. The employees in Sales sorted by name are Dev and Zoya.

questions.q: [Paper A] Cascadeless schedules forbid
questions.why: Cascadeless schedules forbid dirty reads, so no transaction reads data written by an uncommitted transaction.

questions.q: [Paper A] Which index type must be dense?
questions.why: A secondary index is on a non-ordering field, so it needs an entry for every record: it must be dense.

questions.q: [Paper B] R(A,B,C,D) with key A only: number of superkeys
questions.why: A is the only key, so every superkey contains A, and B, C and D are free: 2³ = 8 superkeys.

questions.q: [Paper B] R(A,B,C,D), F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}: candidate keys
questions.why: B never appears on a right side, so it's in every key. AB⁺ = ABCD, BC⁺ = BCDA (C → D, D → A, then AB → C), and BD⁺ = BDAC. So the keys are AB, BC and BD.

questions.q: [Paper B] Same relation: highest NF
questions.why: All attributes are prime, so 3NF holds; C → D and D → A have non-superkey LHS → not BCNF.

questions.q: [Paper B] T1 (3 ops) and T2 (2 ops): number of interleavings
questions.why: Interleavings of 3 and 2 operations: choose which 2 of 5 positions belong to T2: C(5,2) = 5!/(3!2!) = 10.

questions.q: [Paper B] S: R1(A) W2(A) W1(A) — conflict serializable?
questions.why: R1(A) before W2(A) gives T1 → T2, and W2(A) before W1(A) gives T2 → T1. That's a cycle, so it isn't conflict serializable.

questions.q: [Paper B] Block 1024, key 10, block pointer 6: B+ internal order
questions.why: An internal node has p pointers and p − 1 keys: 6p + 10(p − 1) ≤ 1024 → 16p ≤ 1034 → p = 64.

questions.q: [Paper B] File 40,000 records, bfr 20 → blocks; binary search cost
questions.why: 40,000/20 = 2000 blocks. Binary search takes ⌈log₂ 2000⌉ = 11 block reads (2¹⁰ = 1024 < 2000 ≤ 2048 = 2¹¹).

questions.q: [Paper B] `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp e1 JOIN emp e2 ON e1.dept = e2.dept;`
questions.why: Self-join on dept pairs each employee with every employee of the same department, including themselves. Each department has 2 employees, giving 2 × 2 = 4 pairs, and 3 departments give 12.

questions.q: [Paper B] R(A,B,C,D,E), F = {A → B, B → C, C → D, D → E}; decomposition (A,B,C), (C,D,E) is
questions.why: The common attribute C determines C, D and E, so it's a key of the second part, which makes the split lossless. A → B and B → C live in the first part, and C → D and D → E in the second, so all FDs are preserved.

questions.q: [Paper B] Wait–die: T8 requests lock held by T4
questions.why: In wait–die, a younger transaction (T8, newer timestamp) requesting a lock held by an older one (T4) dies, which means it's aborted and restarted.

scenes.text: A shop sign says: 'If you spend ₹2000, you get a free bag.' Tara spent ₹1500 and still got a bag. Did the shop lie?
A truth table for p → q shows the promise is only broken when p is true and q is false. The shop is honest.

steps.title: Connectives
steps.body:
A **proposition** is a statement that is true or false.
- ¬p (not), p ∧ q (and), p ∨ q (or), p ⊕ q (xor)
- **p → q** is false only when p = T and q = F
- **p ↔ q** is true when both have the same value

For p → q: converse q → p, inverse ¬p → ¬q, **contrapositive ¬q → ¬p (equivalent)**.

steps.title: Solved example: truth table
steps.body:
(p → q) ∧ (q → p):
- TT: T∧T = T
- TF: F∧T = F
- FT: T∧F = F
- FF: T∧T = T
Same as p ↔ q ✔. A formula with n variables has 2ⁿ rows.

steps.title: Solved example: tautology
steps.body:
Is (p ∧ (p → q)) → q a tautology?
- The only way to make it false: p ∧ (p → q) = T and q = F. Then p = T and p → q = T forces q = T — contradiction.
- So it is always true: **modus ponens** is a tautology.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking p → q is false when p is false.
- Treating the converse as equivalent to the original.
- Reading 'p unless q' wrongly: it means ¬q → p, i.e. p ∨ q.
- 'p only if q' means p → q, not q → p.

steps.title: Precedence
steps.body: ¬ binds tightest, then ∧, ∨, →, ↔. p → q → r is read p → (q → r).

activity.prompt: Print the truth table of p → q as four lines in the order TT, TF, FT, FF, each line like `T T T` (p q result).

tests.expect:
T T T
T F F
F T T
F F T

activity.hint: p → q equals (!p) || q.

quiz.why: An implication p → q is false only when p is true and q is false (a promise made but broken).
The contrapositive of p → q is ¬q → ¬p, which always has the same truth value.

quiz.q: Rows in a truth table with 4 variables
quiz.why: A truth table has 2ⁿ rows for n variables. For 4 variables that is 2⁴ = 16.
p ⊕ q (exclusive or) is true when exactly one of p and q is true.
'p only if q' means p → q: q is necessary for p.

scenes.text: A lab circuit lights a bulb for ¬(¬p ∨ ¬q) ∨ (p ∧ ¬q). It uses five gates.
Using logical laws, Ved simplifies it to just p — one wire, no gates.

steps.title: Key laws
steps.body:
- **De Morgan**: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q; ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q
- **Implication**: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q
- **Distributive**: p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r)
- **Absorption**: p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p
- Double negation, idempotent, identity, domination, complement

steps.title: Solved example: simplify
steps.body:
¬(¬p ∨ ¬q) ∨ (p ∧ ¬q)
- Step 1 (De Morgan): (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ ¬q)
- Step 2 (distributive): p ∧ (q ∨ ¬q)
- Step 3 (complement): p ∧ T = **p**.

steps.title: CNF and DNF
steps.body:
- **DNF**: OR of ANDs (sum of products). Read from rows where the formula is T.
- **CNF**: AND of ORs (product of sums). Read from rows where the formula is F, negating each literal.
- Every formula has both; SAT is about CNF.

steps.title: Solved example: p ↔ q
steps.body:
True rows: TT, FF → DNF = (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q).
False rows: TF, FT → CNF = (¬p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ ¬q).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- De Morgan without flipping ∧/∨.
- Writing ¬(p → q) ≡ ¬p → ¬q (correct: p ∧ ¬q).
- In CNF from false rows, forgetting to negate literals.

activity.prompt: Read a 2-variable formula's 4 outputs (for rows TT, TF, FT, FF as 1/0). Print its DNF using p, q, ~ for NOT, & and |, with minterms in row order joined by ` | `, each in brackets like `(p & q)`. Print FALSE if no true rows.
activity.hint: Each true row becomes one minterm.

quiz.why: By De Morgan's law, ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q.
Since p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q, its negation is p ∧ ¬q.
By the absorption law, p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p. If p is true the whole is true; if false, both sides are false.

quiz.q: DNF is built from rows where the formula is
quiz.why: The disjunctive normal form is built from the rows where the formula is true: one minterm for each true row.
By the implication law, p → q is equivalent to ¬p ∨ q.

scenes.text: The principal says: 'Every student has a phone.' Mihir wants to disprove it.
He needs just one student without a phone — negating ∀ gives ∃.

steps.title: Quantifiers
steps.body:
P(x) is a predicate over a domain.
- ∀x P(x): true for every x. ∃x P(x): true for some x.
- **Negation**: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x); ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x).
- Order matters: ∀x ∃y (y > x) is true on integers; ∃y ∀x (y > x) is false.

steps.title: Solved example: negate
steps.body:
'Every course has a student who passed.' ∀c ∃s Passed(s, c).
- Negation: ∃c ∀s ¬Passed(s, c) → 'Some course has no student who passed.'

'All birds fly': ∀x (Bird(x) → Flies(x)). Negation: ∃x (Bird(x) ∧ ¬Flies(x)).

steps.title: Rules of inference
steps.body:
- Modus ponens: p, p → q ⊢ q
- Modus tollens: ¬q, p → q ⊢ ¬p
- Hypothetical syllogism: p → q, q → r ⊢ p → r
- Disjunctive syllogism: p ∨ q, ¬p ⊢ q
- Resolution: p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ r ⊢ q ∨ r
- Universal instantiation / existential generalisation

steps.title: Solved example: argument
steps.body:
Premises: 'If it rains, the match is cancelled.' 'The match is not cancelled.' Conclusion?
- r → c, ¬c ⊢ ¬r by **modus tollens**: it did not rain.

Invalid pattern: r → c, c ⊢ r (affirming the consequent).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Translating 'All A are B' as ∀x (A(x) ∧ B(x)) — use →.
- Translating 'Some A are B' as ∃x (A(x) → B(x)) — use ∧.
- Swapping the order of mixed quantifiers.

activity.prompt: Domain = the n integers given. Read n and the numbers. Print two lines: whether ∀x (x > 0) holds (TRUE/FALSE) and whether ∃x (x is even) holds.
activity.hint: ∀ is a big AND; ∃ is a big OR.

quiz.why: Negating a universal statement gives an existential one: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x).
'Some students are athletes' is ∃x (S(x) ∧ A(x)). Using → with ∃ would be wrong, since it's true whenever something isn't a student.
From p → q and ¬q, we conclude ¬p. This valid rule is modus tollens.
From p → q and q, concluding p is the fallacy of affirming the consequent. q could be true for other reasons.
For every integer x there exists y = x + 1, so the statement is true. Here y may depend on x.

scenes.text: Students line up 500 dominoes in the hostel corridor. They are sure all will fall.
Why? The first one falls, and each falling domino knocks the next. That is induction.

steps.title: Proof methods
steps.body:
- **Direct**: assume p, derive q.
- **Contrapositive**: assume ¬q, derive ¬p.
- **Contradiction**: assume ¬(statement), derive a contradiction.
- **Cases**, **counterexample** (to disprove ∀), **constructive / non-constructive existence**.

steps.title: Solved example: √2 is irrational
steps.body:
- Suppose √2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then a² = 2b², so a² is even → a is even, a = 2k.
- 4k² = 2b² → b² = 2k² → b is even.
- Both even contradicts lowest terms. ∎ (contradiction)

Contrapositive example: if n² is even then n is even. Contrapositive: n odd ⇒ n² = (2k+1)² = 2(2k²+2k)+1 odd ✔.

steps.title: Induction
steps.body:
To prove P(n) for all n ≥ n₀:
- **Basis**: P(n₀).
- **Inductive step**: P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) for every k ≥ n₀.
**Strong induction** assumes P(n₀), …, P(k). Structural induction works on trees, strings, formulas.

steps.title: Solved example: sum of odd numbers
steps.body:
Claim: 1 + 3 + … + (2n − 1) = n².
- Basis n = 1: 1 = 1² ✔.
- Step: assume true for k. Then sum to k+1 = k² + (2k + 1) = (k + 1)² ✔. ∎

Another: 2ⁿ > n for n ≥ 1: 2^(k+1) = 2·2^k > 2k ≥ k + 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping the basis (the 'all horses are the same colour' fallacy fails at n = 2).
- Assuming what you want to prove in the inductive step.
- Proving a ∀ statement with examples.

activity.prompt: Read n. Check the identity 1+3+…+(2n−1) = n² by computing the left side with a loop. Print `sum=<s> square=<n*n> OK` (or MISMATCH).
activity.hint: A program checks instances; induction proves all n.

quiz.q: To disprove 'all primes are odd' you need
quiz.why: To disprove a universal claim, one counterexample is enough. 2 is a prime that isn't odd.
Induction needs a basis step (the first case) and an inductive step (if it holds for k, it holds for k + 1).

quiz.q: Proving ¬q → ¬p to show p → q is
quiz.why: Proving ¬q → ¬p to establish p → q is a proof by contrapositive, since they are equivalent.
The sum 1 + 2 + … + n equals n(n + 1)/2 (Gauss's formula).
Strong induction assumes the statement for all earlier cases, P(n₀) through P(k), to prove P(k + 1).

questions.q: Which is a tautology?
questions.why: p ∨ ¬p is always true (law of excluded middle), so it's a tautology.
The implication p → q is equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p.

questions.q: Number of non-equivalent propositions in 2 variables
questions.why: A truth table of 2 variables has 4 rows, and each row can be T or F, so there are 2⁴ = 16 distinct functions.
¬(p ↔ q) is true exactly when p and q have different truth values, which is p ⊕ q.
(p → q) ∧ (p → r) says p implies both, which is p → (q ∧ r).

questions.q: Negation of ∀x ∃y P(x, y)
questions.why: To negate, flip each quantifier and negate the predicate: ¬∀x∃y P ≡ ∃x∀y ¬P.

questions.q: Assertion: (p ∧ (p → q)) → q is a tautology. Reason: modus ponens is a valid rule of inference.
questions.why: A is true: (p ∧ (p → q)) → q is a tautology. R is true and gives the reason: it is modus ponens written as a formula. So R explains A.

questions.q: CNF of p ↔ q
questions.why: p ↔ q is false in the rows (p=T, q=F) and (p=F, q=T). The CNF takes a clause for each false row: (¬p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ ¬q).

questions.q: Resolution of (p ∨ q) and (¬p ∨ r)
questions.why: Resolution: from (p ∨ q) and (¬p ∨ r), the p and ¬p cancel, giving q ∨ r.

questions.q: Case: 'If the server is up then the site loads. The site does not load.' Valid conclusion
questions.why: From 'if the server is up then the site loads' and 'the site doesn't load', modus tollens gives 'the server is not up'.

questions.q: Which is NOT valid?
options: p → q, q → r ⊢ p → r
questions.why: p → q, q ⊢ p is the fallacy of affirming the consequent. The other three are valid rules.

questions.q: On positive integers, ∃x ∀y (x ≤ y) is
questions.why: On positive integers, x = 1 is less than or equal to every y, so ∃x∀y (x ≤ y) is true.

questions.q: On integers, ∃x ∀y (x ≤ y) is
questions.why: The integers have no least element, so no x is ≤ every y, and the statement is false.

questions.q: Induction proves Σ i³ (i=1..n) equals
questions.why: The sum of the first n cubes is (n(n + 1)/2)², which is the square of the sum of the first n integers (Nicomachus).

questions.q: For n ≥ 4, 2ⁿ ≥ n² — basis to check
questions.why: The claim starts at n = 4, so the basis is n = 4: 2⁴ = 16 ≥ 4² = 16. It fails at n = 3 (8 < 9).

questions.q: How many rows of (p ∨ q) → r are false?
questions.why: (p ∨ q) → r is false only when p ∨ q is true and r is false. There are 3 such rows: (p, q) = TT, TF, FT, with r = F.

questions.q: A formula is satisfiable but not valid. Then its negation is
questions.why: If a formula is true in some rows and false in others, flipping every row gives a negation that is also true in some and false in others, so it's satisfiable but not valid.

questions.q: p NAND p ≡
questions.why: p NAND p = ¬(p ∧ p) = ¬p.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Sets, Relations and Functions
courses.summary: Sets and set operations, power sets and Cartesian products, relations and their properties, equivalence relations and partitions, closures and Warshall's algorithm, functions (injective, surjective, bijective), composition and inverses, and countability.
outcomes: Learners can prove set identities and count power sets and products
Learners can test reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive properties
Learners can find equivalence classes and transitive closures
Learners can classify functions and count them

scenes.text: In a class of 60, 25 are in the drama club, 30 in coding club and 10 in both. The teacher asks how many are in neither.
A Venn diagram and |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| answer it: 60 − 45 = 15.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
- Union A ∪ B, intersection A ∩ B, difference A − B, complement Aᶜ, symmetric difference A ⊕ B = (A − B) ∪ (B − A).
- **Power set** P(A): all subsets; |P(A)| = 2^|A|.
- **Cartesian product** A × B: ordered pairs; |A × B| = |A|·|B|.
- Set identities mirror logic: De Morgan (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ.

steps.title: Solved example: prove an identity
steps.body:
Show A − (B ∪ C) = (A − B) ∩ (A − C).
- x ∈ LHS ⇔ x ∈ A ∧ ¬(x ∈ B ∨ x ∈ C) ⇔ x ∈ A ∧ x ∉ B ∧ x ∉ C
- ⇔ (x ∈ A ∧ x ∉ B) ∧ (x ∈ A ∧ x ∉ C) ⇔ x ∈ RHS ∎

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing ∈ (element) with ⊆ (subset): ∅ ⊆ A always, but ∅ ∈ A only if listed.
- |P(∅)| = 1 (not 0).
- A × B ≠ B × A unless A = B or one is empty.

activity.prompt: Read n and n distinct integers (n ≤ 10). Print all subsets of the set (the power set), one per line, using bitmasks from 0 to 2^n − 1; print elements in input order inside braces like {1,3}; the empty set is {}.
activity.hint: Bit i of the mask decides whether a[i] is in the subset.

quiz.why: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, so |P(A)| = 2⁵ = 32.
The Cartesian product has |A| × |B| = 3 × 4 = 12 pairs.
P(∅) = {∅}, which has exactly 1 element, since the empty set has only one subset: itself.
By inclusion–exclusion, those in at least one are 25 + 30 − 10 = 45. So 60 − 45 = 15 do neither.
By De Morgan's law, (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ.

scenes.text: On a social app, 'follows' is a relation: Ana follows Ben does not mean Ben follows Ana.
On a messaging app, 'is a contact of' is symmetric. The properties decide which algorithms apply.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
A relation R on A is a subset of A × A. Represent as a set of pairs, a 0/1 matrix or a digraph.
- **Reflexive**: (a, a) ∈ R ∀a (matrix diagonal all 1)
- **Symmetric**: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R (matrix = transpose)
- **Antisymmetric**: (a, b), (b, a) ∈ R ⇒ a = b
- **Transitive**: (a, b), (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,1)}.
- Reflexive ✔, symmetric ✔, transitive ✔ (check (1,2),(2,1) → (1,1) ✔), antisymmetric ✗ (1 ≠ 2).
- '≤' on integers: reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive, not symmetric.

steps.title: Solved example: counting relations
steps.body:
|A| = n.
- All relations: 2^(n²)
- Reflexive: 2^(n² − n)
- Symmetric: 2^(n(n+1)/2)
- Antisymmetric: 2ⁿ · 3^(n(n−1)/2)
For n = 3: 512, 64, 64, 216.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking antisymmetric means 'not symmetric' — a relation can be both (e.g. equality) or neither.
- The empty relation on a non-empty set is symmetric and transitive but **not** reflexive.
- Missing one pair when checking transitivity — check every (a,b),(b,c) chain.

activity.prompt: Read n and an n×n 0/1 matrix of a relation. Print four lines: R S A T, each followed by YES/NO, for reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive.

tests.expect:
R YES
S YES
A NO
T YES

R NO
S NO
A YES
T YES

activity.hint: Transitivity needs a triple loop.

quiz.q: Number of relations on a 2-element set
quiz.why: A relation on a 2-element set is any subset of the 4 pairs in A × A, so there are 2⁴ = 16.
Divisibility is reflexive (a | a), antisymmetric (a | b and b | a imply a = b) and transitive. That makes it a partial order.
An empty relation lacks (1,1) and (2,2), so it isn't reflexive.
A symmetric relation on 3 elements chooses freely for 3 diagonal pairs and 3 off-diagonal unordered pairs: 6 free choices, so 2⁶ = 64.

quiz.q: Equality relation is symmetric and antisymmetric?
quiz.why: Equality contains only pairs (a, a). Those are symmetric and antisymmetric at the same time.

scenes.text: A PT teacher splits roll numbers into 3 teams by remainder when divided by 3.
Every student lands in exactly one team — an equivalence relation creates a partition.

steps.title: Equivalence relation
steps.body:
Reflexive + symmetric + transitive. Equivalence class [a] = {x : x R a}. The classes form a **partition** of A (non-empty, disjoint, covering), and every partition defines an equivalence relation.

Example: a ≡ b (mod n) has n classes [0], …, [n−1].

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
On {1, …, 6}, aRb ⇔ a ≡ b (mod 3).
- [1] = {1, 4}, [2] = {2, 5}, [3] = {3, 6}.
- Number of equivalence relations on a 3-element set = number of partitions = **Bell number B₃ = 5**. (B₄ = 15.)

steps.title: Closures
steps.body:
- Reflexive closure: R ∪ {(a, a)}.
- Symmetric closure: R ∪ R⁻¹.
- **Transitive closure** R⁺: add (a, c) whenever a path a → … → c exists. **Warshall's algorithm**: for k, for i, for j: W[i][j] |= W[i][k] & W[k][j] — O(n³).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting k as the inner loop in Warshall.
- Thinking the union of two equivalence relations is an equivalence relation (not always transitive).
- Forgetting that classes must be non-empty.

activity.prompt: Read n and an n×n 0/1 matrix. Print the matrix of its transitive closure (Warshall), rows on separate lines, entries space separated.
activity.hint: k outermost.

quiz.why: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

quiz.q: Number of equivalence relations on {a, b, c}
quiz.why: Equivalence relations correspond to partitions. A 3-element set has 5 partitions (the Bell number B₃ = 5).

quiz.q: Classes of congruence mod 5 on integers
quiz.why: Congruence mod 5 splits the integers by remainder 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, which gives 5 classes.
Warshall's algorithm has three nested loops over n elements, so it takes O(n³) time.
The symmetric closure adds the reverse of every pair: R ∪ R⁻¹.

scenes.text: Every student gets one roll number and no two students share one. The office calls it a one-to-one mapping.
A maths club debate: are there 'more' real numbers than whole numbers? Cantor's diagonal argument says yes.

steps.title: Kinds of functions
steps.body:
f: A → B assigns exactly one b to each a.
- **Injective** (one-one): f(a₁) = f(a₂) ⇒ a₁ = a₂.
- **Surjective** (onto): every b has a pre-image.
- **Bijective**: both; then f⁻¹ exists.
- Composition (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)); composition of bijections is a bijection.

steps.title: Solved example: counting functions
steps.body:
|A| = m, |B| = n.
- All functions: nᵐ.
- Injective (m ≤ n): n!/(n − m)!.
- Bijective (m = n): n!.
- Surjective: Σ (−1)^k C(n, k)(n − k)ᵐ. For m = 4, n = 2: 16 − 2 = **14**; for m = 3, n = 3: 6.

steps.title: Solved example: classify
steps.body:
- f(x) = 2x + 3 on ℝ → bijective; f⁻¹(y) = (y − 3)/2.
- f(x) = x² on ℝ → neither (f(−1) = f(1); −1 not reached).
- f(x) = x² on [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) → bijective.
- f(n) = 2n on ℤ → injective, not onto ℤ (odd numbers missing).

steps.title: Countability
steps.body: A set is **countable** if it is finite or in bijection with ℕ. ℤ and ℚ are countable; ℝ and P(ℕ) are **uncountable** (Cantor's diagonal argument). Consequence: some problems have no algorithm — programs are countable, problems are not.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to check the codomain when testing 'onto'.
- Applying the pigeonhole principle backwards: injective needs |A| ≤ |B|.
- Calling ℚ uncountable because it is dense.

activity.prompt: Read m and n. Print the number of surjective functions from an m-set onto an n-set using inclusion–exclusion (m, n ≤ 15; use long long).
activity.hint: Subtract functions missing at least one target, add back double-counted ones…

quiz.why: Each of the 3 inputs can map to any of 4 outputs: 4³ = 64 functions.

quiz.q: Injective functions from a 2-set to a 4-set
quiz.why: For an injective function, the first element has 4 choices and the second 3 remaining: 4 × 3 = 12.
x³ is strictly increasing, so it is one-to-one, and it takes every real value, so it's onto. It's bijective.
By Cantor's diagonal argument, ℝ is uncountable. ℤ, ℚ and the even numbers are countable.
There are 2⁴ = 16 functions from a 4-set to a 2-set. Remove the 2 constant functions, which aren't onto: 14.

questions.why: P(∅) = {∅} has 1 element, so P(P(∅)) has 2¹ = 2 elements.
The symmetric difference contains elements in exactly one of the sets: 1 (only in A) and 4 (only in B). So {1, 4}.

questions.q: Reflexive relations on a 4-element set
questions.why: A reflexive relation must contain all 4 diagonal pairs and may include any of the other 16 − 4 = 12 pairs: 2¹² relations.

questions.q: Relations on a 3-set that are both reflexive and symmetric
questions.why: Reflexive fixes the diagonal. Symmetry means the 3 off-diagonal pairs {a,b} are each in or out: 2³ = 8.

questions.q: Equivalence relations on a 4-element set
questions.why: The number of equivalence relations on a 4-element set is the Bell number B₄ = 15.

questions.q: Assertion: every partition of A defines an equivalence relation. Reason: 'in the same block' is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
questions.why: A is true: a partition defines an equivalence relation. R is true and explains it: 'in the same block' is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
R is symmetric, but it lacks (1,1) and (2,2), so it isn't reflexive. It isn't transitive either: (1,2) and (2,1) would force (1,1).

questions.q: Transitive closure of {(1,2),(2,3),(3,1)} on {1,2,3} has how many pairs
questions.why: The relation is a 3-cycle, so every element reaches every element, including itself, after enough steps. The closure has all 3 × 3 = 9 pairs.

questions.q: f: ℤ → ℤ, f(n) = n + 5 is
questions.why: f(n) = n + 5 is one-to-one, and every integer m is hit by m − 5. So it's bijective.

questions.q: Bijections from a 5-set to itself
questions.why: Bijections of a 5-set onto itself are its permutations: 5! = 120.

questions.q: Case: 70 students: 40 take Python, 35 Java, 15 both. How many take neither?
questions.why: Students taking at least one: 40 + 35 − 15 = 60. So 70 − 60 = 10 take neither.

questions.q: |A ∪ B ∪ C| with |A|=|B|=|C|=10, pairwise intersections 3 each, triple 1
questions.why: By inclusion–exclusion: 30 − (3 + 3 + 3) + 1 = 22.

questions.q: If g ∘ f is injective then
questions.why: If g ∘ f is injective, then f(a) = f(b) gives g(f(a)) = g(f(b)), so a = b. Hence f must be injective.

questions.q: If g ∘ f is surjective then
questions.why: If g ∘ f is surjective, every element of the final set is reached through g, so g must be surjective.

questions.q: Antisymmetric relations on a 2-element set
questions.why: For each diagonal pair, in or out: 2² = 4. For each of the 1 off-diagonal pair {a,b}, there are 3 options (neither, a→b, b→a): 3. Total 4 × 3 = 12.

questions.q: Which is countable?
options: the set of all finite binary strings
questions.why: The finite binary strings can be listed by length and then in order, so they're countable. P(ℕ) and ℝ are uncountable.

questions.q: Number of subsets of a 6-set with exactly 2 elements
questions.why: The number of 2-element subsets of a 6-set is C(6, 2) = 15.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Partial Orders, Lattices and Boolean Algebra
courses.summary: Partially ordered sets and Hasse diagrams, extremal elements, topological sorting of posets, lattices (distributive and complemented), and Boolean algebra with Boolean functions, minterms and Karnaugh-map style simplification.
outcomes: Learners can draw a Hasse diagram and identify maximal, minimal, greatest and least elements
Learners can find LUB and GLB and decide whether a poset is a lattice
Learners can test distributive and complemented lattices
Learners can simplify Boolean expressions and count Boolean functions

scenes.text: A syllabus says some subjects must come before others, but many pairs have no order at all.
A Hasse diagram draws only the 'immediately before' links, so the whole order fits on one page.

steps.title: Partial order
steps.body:
A relation that is **reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive**. (A, ≼) is a **poset**. Elements a, b are *comparable* if a ≼ b or b ≼ a. A **total order** (chain) has every pair comparable.

Examples: (ℤ, ≤) total; (P(S), ⊆) and (ℤ⁺, |) partial.

steps.title: Hasse diagram
steps.body: Draw a ≺ b with b above a; remove self-loops and edges implied by transitivity; drop arrow heads. An edge means b **covers** a (nothing strictly between).

steps.title: Solved example: divisors of 12
steps.body:
D₁₂ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12} under |.
- Covers: 1–2, 1–3, 2–4, 2–6, 3–6, 4–12, 6–12.
- Minimal = least = 1; maximal = greatest = 12.
- 4 and 6 are incomparable; 4 and 3 are incomparable.

steps.title: Extremal elements
steps.body:
- **Maximal**: nothing above it. **Greatest**: above everything (unique if it exists).
- Upper bound of S, **least upper bound (LUB, join ∨)**, lower bound, **greatest lower bound (GLB, meet ∧)**.
- In (ℤ⁺, |): LUB = lcm, GLB = gcd.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing transitive edges in a Hasse diagram.
- Confusing maximal with greatest: {2, 3} under | has two maximal elements and no greatest.
- Forgetting reflexivity — '<' is a strict order, not a partial order.

activity.prompt: Read n. Print every cover pair (a b) of the divisibility poset on the divisors of n, one per line, sorted by a then b, where b covers a means a | b, a ≠ b and no divisor c with a | c | b strictly between.
activity.hint: b covers a iff b/a is prime — or just test all middle divisors.

quiz.q: A partial order is reflexive, transitive and
quiz.why: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive.
In the divisibility order, the least upper bound of two numbers is their lcm. The lcm of 4 and 6 is 12.

quiz.q: Edges in the Hasse diagram of D₆
quiz.why: D₆ = {1, 2, 3, 6}. Its Hasse diagram has edges 1–2, 1–3, 2–6 and 3–6: 4 edges.

quiz.q: A poset {2, 3, 6, 9} under | has maximal elements
quiz.why: A maximal element has nothing above it. 6 and 9 divide nothing else in the set, so both are maximal. 2 and 3 divide 6.

quiz.q: A chain is a poset in which
quiz.why: In a chain (total order), every two elements are comparable.

scenes.text: A government system labels documents with clearance levels and categories.
Any two labels have a lowest common clearance and a highest shared one — a lattice keeps access rules consistent.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A **lattice** is a poset where every pair has both a LUB (a ∨ b) and a GLB (a ∧ b).
- (P(S), ⊆): ∨ = ∪, ∧ = ∩.
- (Dₙ, |): ∨ = lcm, ∧ = gcd.
- Every finite lattice has a greatest element 1 and a least element 0 (bounded).

steps.title: Special lattices
steps.body:
- **Distributive**: a ∧ (b ∨ c) = (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c). A lattice is distributive iff it has no sublattice shaped like **M₃** (diamond with 3 middle elements) or **N₅** (pentagon).
- **Complemented**: every a has a′ with a ∨ a′ = 1 and a ∧ a′ = 0.
- In a distributive lattice, complements are unique.
- **Boolean algebra** = complemented distributive lattice.

steps.title: Solved example: D₃₀ vs D₁₂
steps.body:
- D₃₀ = divisors of 2·3·5: complement of d is 30/d (gcd = 1, lcm = 30) → complemented and distributive → **Boolean algebra** (isomorphic to P({2,3,5})).
- D₁₂: 2 has no complement (needs gcd(2,x) = 1 and lcm = 12 → x = 3 gives lcm 6 ✗) → not complemented.
- Dₙ is Boolean iff n is square-free.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming every poset with 0 and 1 is a lattice — some pair may lack a unique LUB.
- Thinking complements are always unique (fails in M₃ and N₅).
- Calling every Dₙ a Boolean algebra.

activity.prompt: Read n. Print YES if the divisor lattice Dₙ is a Boolean algebra (every divisor d has a complement, i.e. gcd(d, n/d) = 1), else NO.
activity.hint: The complement of d must be n/d.

quiz.why: In the subset lattice, the greatest lower bound (meet) of two sets is their intersection.
D₃₀ is a Boolean algebra because 30 = 2 × 3 × 5 is square-free (a product of distinct primes).

quiz.q: A lattice is distributive iff it has no sublattice isomorphic to
quiz.why: By Birkhoff's criterion, a lattice is distributive exactly when it has no sublattice isomorphic to the diamond M₃ or the pentagon N₅.
The complement of 6 in D₃₀ is 30/6 = 5, since lcm(6, 5) = 30 and gcd(6, 5) = 1.
A Boolean algebra is a complemented distributive lattice.

scenes.text: A lab alarm rings if (door open AND night) OR (door open AND NOT night AND weekend) OR (door open AND night AND weekend).
Boolean algebra reduces it to: door open AND (night OR weekend).

steps.title: Boolean functions
steps.body:
f: {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1}. There are **2^(2ⁿ)** of them (n = 2 → 16, n = 3 → 256).
- Minterm: product with every variable once (true at one row). f = Σm(…) sum of minterms.
- Maxterm: sum with every variable once. f = ΠM(…).
- Duality: swap +/· and 0/1 in an identity to get another identity.

steps.title: Solved example: algebraic simplification
steps.body:
F = d·n + d·n′·w + d·n·w.
- d·n + d·n·w = d·n (absorption).
- F = d·n + d·n′·w = d(n + n′w) = d(n + w) (since n + n′w = n + w).
- **F = d(n + w)**.

steps.title: Solved example: K-map
steps.body:
F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 2, 4, 5, 6).
- Group m0, m2, m4, m6 (the four cells with C = 0) → **C′**.
- Group m4, m5 (A = 1, B = 0) → **AB′**.
- F = C′ + AB′.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Grouping cells that are not adjacent in Gray-code order (00, 01, 11, 10).
- Groups of size 3 or 6 — group sizes must be powers of 2.
- Forgetting the wrap-around adjacency at the edges of a K-map.

activity.prompt: Read 8 bits giving F(A,B,C) for rows 000..111 in order. Print the minterm list like `m(0,2,4)` (or `m()` if none) on one line and the count of 1s on the next.
activity.hint: Row index = binary ABC.

quiz.q: Number of Boolean functions of 3 variables
quiz.why: A Boolean function of 3 variables has 2³ = 8 truth-table rows, each T or F, so 2⁸ = 256 functions.
By the absorption-type identity, x + x′y = x + y.
The dual swaps + and · and swaps 0 and 1. So x + 0 = x becomes x · 1 = x.
A K-map group must contain a power of two cells: 1, 2, 4 or 8 (and so on), so that terms simplify properly.
m5 is binary 101, so A = 1, B = 0, C = 1, giving the minterm AB′C.

scenes.text: A build tool must compile modules so that each comes after the modules it imports.
Any linear extension of the 'imports' partial order is a valid build order.

steps.title: Linear extension
steps.body:
A total order that contains the partial order. Every finite poset has one — **topological sorting**: repeatedly remove a minimal element.

Well-ordered set: every non-empty subset has a least element (ℕ under ≤ is; ℤ is not). Basis of induction.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Poset on {a, b, c, d}: a ≺ b, a ≺ c, b ≺ d, c ≺ d.
- Remove a (minimal) → b, c minimal → remove b → c → d.
- Linear extensions: **a b c d** and **a c b d** (2 in total).

steps.title: Chains and antichains
steps.body:
- Height = longest chain; width = largest antichain.
- **Dilworth's theorem**: width = minimum number of chains needed to cover the poset.
- Mirsky's theorem: height = minimum number of antichains covering it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the linear extension is unique.
- Calling ℤ well-ordered.
- Confusing chain length (edges) with chain size (elements).

activity.prompt: Put the modules in a valid build order: utils is imported by db and api; db is imported by api; api is imported by app.

quiz.q: A linear extension of a finite poset always
quiz.why: Every finite poset has at least one linear extension, found by a topological sort.
ℕ with ≤ is well-ordered: every non-empty subset has a least element.

quiz.q: Largest antichain of P({1,2,3}) under ⊆ has size
quiz.why: The largest antichain in P({1,2,3}) is all three singletons (or all three 2-element subsets), size 3 (Sperner's theorem).

options: minimum number of chains covering the poset
quiz.why: Dilworth's theorem: the width (largest antichain) equals the minimum number of chains needed to cover the poset.

quiz.q: Number of linear extensions of an antichain of 3 elements
quiz.why: In an antichain, no two elements are comparable, so any ordering is a valid linear extension: 3! = 6.

questions.q: Which is NOT a partial order on ℤ⁺?
questions.why: < isn't reflexive (a < a is false), so it isn't a partial order. |, ≤ and = all are.

questions.q: GLB of 12 and 18 in (ℤ⁺, |)
questions.why: In the divisibility order, the greatest lower bound is the gcd. gcd(12, 18) = 6.

questions.q: Hasse diagram edges for P({a,b}) under ⊆
questions.why: The Hasse diagram of P({a, b}) is a square with 4 edges: ∅–{a}, ∅–{b}, {a}–{a,b}, {b}–{a,b}.

questions.q: Hasse edges of P({a,b,c})
questions.why: The Hasse diagram of P(S) with |S| = n has n·2ⁿ⁻¹ edges, so 3 × 4 = 12.

questions.q: D₃₆ is complemented?
questions.why: D₃₆ isn't complemented because 36 = 2² × 3² isn't square-free. For example, 2 has no complement.

questions.q: Assertion: every finite lattice is bounded. Reason: the join of all elements is the greatest element.
questions.why: A is true: every finite lattice is bounded. R is true and explains it: the join of all the elements is the greatest element, and the meet of all of them is the least.

questions.q: Complement of 2 in D₄₂ (42 = 2·3·7)
questions.why: The complement of 2 in D₄₂ is 42/2 = 21, since gcd(2, 21) = 1 and lcm(2, 21) = 42.

questions.q: Number of Boolean functions of 2 variables that are self-dual
questions.why: A self-dual function of n variables is determined by half its truth table, so there are 2^(2ⁿ⁻¹) of them. For n = 2 that's 2² = 4.

questions.q: Simplify A·B + A·B′
Simplify (A + B)(A + B′)
K-map minimal SOP for Σm(1, 3, 5, 7) in A, B, C
questions.why: Minterms 1, 3, 5, 7 are exactly the rows where C = 1, so they group together and the minimal SOP is just C.

questions.q: Case: modules {x, y, z} with no dependencies between them. Number of valid build orders
questions.why: With no dependencies, any order of the 3 modules is valid: 3! = 6.

questions.q: Which lattice is not distributive?
questions.why: The diamond M₃ is the classic non-distributive lattice. Chains, power-set lattices and divisor lattices of square-free numbers are distributive.

questions.q: Maximal elements of {2, 4, 5, 10, 12, 20, 25} under |
questions.why: A maximal element divides nothing else in the set. 12, 20 and 25 qualify, while 2, 4, 5 and 10 each divide one of 12, 20 or 25.

questions.q: Minimal elements of the same set
questions.why: A minimal element has nothing below it. 2 and 5 have no divisors in the set other than themselves, so they're minimal.

questions.q: Number of minterms of F = A + B (2 variables)
questions.why: A + B is true for 01, 10 and 11, so it has 3 minterms (false only for 00).

questions.q: Width of D₃₀ under divisibility
questions.why: The width is the size of the largest antichain. In D₃₀ the sets {2, 3, 5} and {6, 10, 15} have no divisibility between members, size 3.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Combinatorics and Recurrence Relations
courses.summary: Sum and product rules, permutations and combinations with and without repetition, binomial theorem, pigeonhole principle, inclusion–exclusion and derangements, linear recurrence relations with characteristic roots, and generating functions.
outcomes: Learners can choose the right counting formula for a problem
Learners can apply the pigeonhole principle and inclusion–exclusion
Learners can count derangements and distributions (stars and bars)
Learners can solve homogeneous and non-homogeneous linear recurrences

lessons.title: Permutations, combinations and the binomial theorem

scenes.text: An app requires a 6-character PIN of digits. How many PINs exist? A product rule answers instantly: 10⁶.
The student council must pick 3 out of 10 volunteers, order not mattering: C(10, 3) = 120.

steps.title: Core formulas
steps.body:
- **Product rule**: tasks in sequence multiply. **Sum rule**: disjoint alternatives add.
- Permutations: P(n, r) = n!/(n − r)!
- Combinations: C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!)
- With repetition: arrangements nʳ; **multisets** C(n + r − 1, r)
- Words with repeated letters: n!/(n₁! n₂! …)

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- Arrangements of MISSISSIPPI: 11!/(1!·4!·4!·2!) = **34650**.
- 5 people around a round table: (5 − 1)! = **24**.
- Ways to choose 4 scoops from 3 flavours (repetition allowed): C(3 + 4 − 1, 4) = C(6, 4) = **15**.
- Integer solutions of x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 10, xᵢ ≥ 0: C(12, 2) = **66** (stars and bars).

steps.title: Binomial theorem
steps.body:
(x + y)ⁿ = Σ C(n, k) xᵏ yⁿ⁻ᵏ.
- Σ C(n, k) = 2ⁿ; alternating sum = 0.
- Pascal: C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k).
- Coefficient of x³ in (2x − 1)⁵: C(5, 3)·2³·(−1)² = 10·8 = **80**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using permutations when order does not matter (or vice versa).
- Forgetting to divide by repeated letters.
- In stars and bars with xᵢ ≥ 1, substitute yᵢ = xᵢ − 1 first: C(n − 1, k − 1).

activity.prompt: Read n and r (0 ≤ r ≤ n ≤ 60). Print C(n, r) exactly using Pascal's triangle with unsigned long long.

quiz.why: P(5, 2) = 5 × 4 = 20 ordered arrangements of 2 from 5.

quiz.q: Arrangements of the letters of LEVEL
quiz.why: LEVEL has 5 letters with L twice and E twice: 5!/(2! 2!) = 120/4 = 30.

quiz.q: Non-negative solutions of a + b + c = 5
quiz.why: Stars and bars: non-negative solutions of a + b + c = 5 number C(5 + 2, 2) = C(7, 2) = 21.
The sum of C(6, k) for k = 0 to 6 is 2⁶ = 64, the total number of subsets.

scenes.text: In a batch of 400 students, the professor bets that two share a birthday. He cannot lose.
There are only 366 possible birthdays — more pigeons than holes.

steps.title: Pigeonhole
steps.body:
If n items go into k boxes and n > k, some box has ≥ 2. **Generalised**: some box has ≥ ⌈n/k⌉.
- Among any 5 points in a unit square, two are within √2/2 (divide into 4 squares).
- Any n + 1 numbers from {1, …, 2n} include two consecutive (hence coprime) numbers.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
How many students guarantee that at least 6 get the same grade among 5 grades?
- Need ⌈N/5⌉ ≥ 6 → N ≥ 26. Answer **26**.

Socks: 10 black and 10 white in the dark; draws to guarantee a matching pair = **3**.

steps.title: Inclusion–exclusion and derangements
steps.body:
|A₁ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ| = Σ|Aᵢ| − Σ|Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ| + … + (−1)ⁿ⁺¹|A₁ ∩ … ∩ Aₙ|.
- Numbers in 1..100 divisible by 2, 3 or 5: 50 + 33 + 20 − 16 − 10 − 6 + 3 = **74**.
- **Derangements** Dₙ = n! Σ (−1)ᵏ/k! ≈ n!/e; D₁=0, D₂=1, D₃=2, D₄=9, D₅=44. Recurrence Dₙ = (n − 1)(Dₙ₋₁ + Dₙ₋₂).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ⌊n/k⌋ instead of ⌈n/k⌉.
- Stopping inclusion–exclusion after the pairwise terms.
- Confusing 'at least one fixed point' (n! − Dₙ) with derangements.

activity.prompt: Read n (≤ 20). Print the number of derangements Dₙ using Dₙ = (n−1)(Dₙ₋₁ + Dₙ₋₂), D₀ = 1, D₁ = 0.
activity.hint: Start the array with d[0]=1, d[1]=0.

quiz.q: Minimum people to guarantee two share a birth month
quiz.why: With 12 months, 12 people could all have different months. A 13th must repeat one (pigeonhole).
Divisible by 2: 15, by 3: 10, by both (6): 5. By inclusion–exclusion 15 + 10 − 5 = 20.

quiz.q: Generalised pigeonhole: 100 items in 7 boxes; some box has at least
quiz.why: With 100 items in 7 boxes, some box has at least ⌈100/7⌉ = ⌈14.29⌉ = 15 items.
The fraction of permutations that are derangements, Dₙ/n!, tends to 1/e ≈ 0.368 as n grows.

scenes.text: Fibonacci's rabbit puzzle and a bank's EMI schedule both follow rules like aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂ + f(n).
Solving the recurrence gives a closed formula — no need to compute every term.

steps.title: Homogeneous with constant coefficients
steps.body:
aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + … + cₖaₙ₋ₖ. Characteristic equation rᵏ − c₁rᵏ⁻¹ − … − cₖ = 0.
- Distinct roots r₁, r₂: aₙ = A r₁ⁿ + B r₂ⁿ.
- Repeated root r: aₙ = (A + Bn) rⁿ.
Use initial conditions to find A, B.

steps.title: Non-homogeneous
steps.body:
aₙ = (homogeneous solution) + (particular solution).
- f(n) = constant → try a constant; f(n) = cⁿ → try Dcⁿ (multiply by n if c is a root).
- aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + 1, a₀ = 0 → particular −1; aₙ = A2ⁿ − 1 → A = 1 → **aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1** (Tower of Hanoi).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the n factor for repeated roots.
- Choosing a particular solution of the same form as a homogeneous term (must multiply by n).
- Applying initial conditions before adding the particular solution.

activity.prompt: Read n. Compute aₙ from aₙ = 5aₙ₋₁ − 6aₙ₋₂, a₀ = 1, a₁ = 4 iteratively, and also the closed form 2·3ⁿ − 2ⁿ. Print both separated by a space (n ≤ 30).
activity.hint: Keep the last two terms.

quiz.why: The characteristic equation is r² − r − 2 = 0, which factors as (r − 2)(r + 1) = 0. So the roots are 2 and −1.

quiz.q: Solution form for a double root 3
quiz.why: For a double root r = 3, the general solution is (A + Bn)3ⁿ, where the factor n handles the repeated root.
The terms are a₁ = 1, a₂ = 3, a₃ = 7, a₄ = 15, a₅ = 31, which fit aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1. So a₅ = 31.
Each term is 3 times the previous one, a geometric sequence with first term 2: aₙ = 2 · 3ⁿ.

quiz.q: For aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + 2ⁿ, the particular solution should be tried as
quiz.why: Since 2 is already a root of the homogeneous part, try a particular solution of the form D·n·2ⁿ, not D·2ⁿ.

scenes.text: A shopkeeper wonders how many ways she can make ₹10 using ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins.
Multiplying three power series and reading off one coefficient gives the answer: 10.

steps.title: Ordinary generating function
steps.body:
G(x) = Σ aₙ xⁿ encodes a sequence.
- 1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + … (all 1s)
- 1/(1 − x)ᵏ = Σ C(n + k − 1, n) xⁿ
- Product of GFs ↔ combining independent choices.

steps.title: Solved example: coins
steps.body:
Ways to pay n with coins 1, 2, 5 = coefficient of xⁿ in 1/((1 − x)(1 − x²)(1 − x⁵)).
- For n = 10: count (fives, twos): fives = 0 → 6 ways (twos 0..5), fives = 1 → 3 ways (twos 0..2), fives = 2 → 1 way → **10**.

steps.title: Catalan numbers
steps.body:
Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n + 1): 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132.
Counts: balanced parenthesis strings of n pairs, binary trees with n nodes, triangulations of an (n + 2)-gon, monotone lattice paths not crossing the diagonal, stack-permutations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting ordered coin sequences when the problem wants unordered (that's a different GF).
- Off-by-one in Catalan index (C₃ = 5, not C₂).
- Treating GF manipulation as needing convergence — for counting we use formal power series.

activity.prompt: Read k coin values and an amount n (≤ 1000). Print the number of ways to make n (order does not matter) — the coefficient of xⁿ in the product of 1/(1 − x^c).
activity.hint: Loop coins outside, amounts inside (that counts combinations, not orders).

quiz.why: The generating function of 1, 1, 1, … is 1 + x + x² + … = 1/(1 − x).
The Catalan number Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n + 1), so C₄ = C(8, 4)/5 = 70/5 = 14.

quiz.q: Balanced strings with 3 pairs of brackets
quiz.why: The number of balanced bracket strings with n pairs is the Catalan number Cₙ. For 3 pairs, C₃ = 5.
The coefficient of xᵏ in 1/(1 − x)³ is C(k + 2, 2). For k = 2, C(4, 2) = 6.

quiz.q: Ways to make 7 with coins 2 and 3 (unordered)
quiz.why: To make 7 with coins of 2 and 3, use 2a + 3b = 7. The only non-negative solution is a = 2, b = 1 (2 + 2 + 3), so 1 way.

questions.q: Number of 4-letter strings from 26 letters with no repeats
Number of ways to seat 6 people around a round table
questions.why: Round-table arrangements of n people number (n − 1)! since rotations count as the same. For 6 people, 5! = 120.

questions.q: Positive integer solutions of x + y + z = 10
questions.why: Positive solutions of x + y + z = 10 equal non-negative solutions of a + b + c = 7: C(9, 2) = 36.

questions.q: Coefficient of x⁵ in (1 + x)¹⁰
questions.why: The coefficient of x⁵ in (1 + x)¹⁰ is C(10, 5) = 252.

questions.q: Integers in 1..1000 divisible by none of 2, 3, 5
questions.why: By inclusion–exclusion, the number divisible by 2, 3 or 5 is 500 + 333 + 200 − 166 − 100 − 66 + 33 = 734. So 1000 − 734 = 266 are divisible by none.

questions.q: D₆
Assertion: among any 11 integers, two have the same last digit. Reason: there are 10 possible last digits.
questions.why: A is true: among 11 integers two share a last digit. R is true and explains it: there are only 10 possible last digits (boxes), so by pigeonhole 11 numbers force a repeat.

questions.q: Solve aₙ = 6aₙ₋₁ − 9aₙ₋₂, a₀ = 1, a₁ = 6
questions.why: The characteristic equation r² − 6r + 9 = 0 has a double root 3, so aₙ = (A + Bn)3ⁿ. a₀ = 1 gives A = 1, and a₁ = 6 gives (1 + B) × 3 = 6, so B = 1. So aₙ = (1 + n)3ⁿ.

questions.q: Number of bit strings of length 8 with exactly three 1s
questions.why: Choose the positions of the three 1s among 8: C(8, 3) = 56.

questions.q: Bit strings of length n with no two consecutive 1s satisfy
questions.why: A valid string of length n ends in 0 (any valid string of length n − 1 before it) or in 01 (any valid string of length n − 2). So aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂, a Fibonacci-type recurrence.

questions.q: Bit strings of length n with no two consecutive 1s satisfy aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂, with a₁ = 2 and a₂ = 3. Find a₄.
Case: a lab has 5 identical laptops for 3 different teams, each team may get zero. Ways
questions.why: Identical laptops to different teams, with zero allowed, is non-negative solutions of a + b + c = 5: C(7, 2) = 21.

questions.q: Number of onto functions from a 5-set to a 3-set
questions.why: By inclusion–exclusion, onto functions from a 5-set to a 3-set number 3⁵ − 3 × 2⁵ + 3 × 1 = 243 − 96 + 3 = 150.

questions.q: Number of monotone lattice paths from (0,0) to (4,4)
questions.why: A path to (4, 4) has 8 steps, 4 right and 4 up. Choose which 4 are right: C(8, 4) = 70.

questions.q: …of those, paths never going above the diagonal
questions.why: Paths from (0,0) to (n, n) that never go above the diagonal are counted by the Catalan number Cₙ. For n = 4 it's 14.

questions.q: Minimum number of cards drawn from a standard 52-card deck to guarantee 3 of the same suit
questions.why: In the worst case you draw 2 of each suit (8 cards) without 3 of any. The 9th card must make 3 of one suit: 2 × 4 + 1 = 9.

questions.q: Particular solution of aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 4
questions.why: A constant particular solution c must satisfy c = 3c + 4. Then −2c = 4, so c = −2. Check: −2 = 3(−2) + 4 = −2.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Graph Theory
courses.summary: Graph types, degree sequences and the handshake lemma, isomorphism, connectivity, Euler and Hamiltonian graphs, trees and spanning trees (Cayley's formula), planarity and Euler's formula, colouring and matchings.
outcomes: Learners can test degree sequences and isomorphism invariants
Learners can apply Euler's and Dirac's/Ore's conditions
Learners can use Euler's formula and its edge bounds for planar graphs
Learners can compute chromatic numbers and matchings in small graphs

scenes.text: At the farewell party everyone shakes hands with some people. Kavya claims exactly 7 people shook an odd number of hands.
Her friend says that is impossible — the number of odd-degree people is always even.

steps.title: Degrees
steps.body:
**Handshake lemma**: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|. Hence the number of odd-degree vertices is even.
- Degree sequence test: **Havel–Hakimi** — remove the largest d, subtract 1 from the next d entries, repeat; graphical iff you reach all zeros.

steps.title: Special graphs
steps.body:
- Kₙ: n(n−1)/2 edges. Cₙ: n edges. Wheel Wₙ. Hypercube Qₙ: 2ⁿ vertices, n·2ⁿ⁻¹ edges.
- Bipartite K_{m,n}: mn edges. A graph is bipartite iff it has no odd cycle.
- k-regular graph on n vertices has nk/2 edges (so nk must be even).
- Complement Ḡ has n(n−1)/2 − |E| edges.

steps.title: Solved example: Havel–Hakimi
steps.body:
Is (3, 3, 2, 2, 2) graphical?
- Remove 3 → subtract from next three: (2, 1, 1, 2) → sort (2, 2, 1, 1).
- Remove 2 → (1, 0, 1) → sort (1, 1, 0). Remove 1 → (0, 0). ✔ **Graphical**.
- (3, 3, 3, 1): remove 3 → (2, 2, 0); remove 2 → (1, −1) ✗ **not graphical**.

steps.title: Isomorphism
steps.body: G ≅ H if a bijection of vertices preserves adjacency. Necessary invariants: same number of vertices, edges, degree sequence, number of cycles of each length, bipartiteness, connectivity. Invariants can show *non*-isomorphism; proving isomorphism needs an explicit bijection.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding isomorphism from equal degree sequences alone.
- Forgetting the handshake parity check (an odd degree sum is impossible).
- Mixing up Qₙ's vertex and edge counts.

activity.prompt: Read n and a degree sequence of n non-negative integers. Print YES if it is graphical (Havel–Hakimi), else NO.
activity.hint: Sort descending each round.

quiz.why: Qₙ has n·2ⁿ⁻¹ edges (each of 2ⁿ vertices has degree n, and each edge is counted twice). For Q₃ this gives 3·2² = 12.
Every vertex of one part joins to every vertex of the other, so K_{m,n} has m·n edges. Here 3·4 = 12; adding 3+4 is a common slip.
The degree sum must equal 2E, so it must be even. 3·7 = 21 is odd, so no 3-regular graph on 7 vertices exists (it would need 10.5 edges).

quiz.q: Complement of a graph with 6 vertices and 5 edges has
quiz.why: A graph and its complement together make all C(6,2) = 15 possible edges. So the complement has 15 − 5 = 10 edges.
Equal degree sequences are necessary for isomorphism but not sufficient. Two different graphs, such as one 6-cycle versus two triangles, can share the same degrees.

scenes.text: In 18th-century Königsberg, people tried to cross all seven bridges exactly once in one walk.
Euler proved it impossible: four land masses all had odd degree. Graph theory was born.

steps.title: Euler
steps.body:
Connected graph (ignoring isolated vertices):
- **Euler circuit** iff every vertex has even degree.
- **Euler path** (not circuit) iff exactly two vertices have odd degree — start at one, end at the other.
- Directed: circuit iff in-degree = out-degree everywhere (and connected).
Fleury's / Hierholzer's algorithm finds it in O(E).

steps.title: Hamilton
steps.body:
No simple characterisation (NP-complete). Sufficient conditions for n ≥ 3:
- **Dirac**: every deg(v) ≥ n/2.
- **Ore**: deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n for every non-adjacent pair.
Kₙ (n ≥ 3) is Hamiltonian; K_{m,n} is Hamiltonian iff m = n ≥ 2.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- Königsberg degrees (5, 3, 3, 3): four odd → **no Euler path**.
- K₅: all degrees 4 → Euler circuit ✔; Dirac 4 ≥ 2.5 → Hamiltonian ✔.
- K₄: degrees 3 (four odd) → no Euler path; but Hamiltonian ✔.
- Petersen graph: 3-regular, 10 vertices — **not** Hamiltonian (classic counterexample).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating Dirac's condition as necessary (C₅ is Hamiltonian with degrees 2 < 2.5).
- Forgetting the connectivity requirement for Euler circuits.
- Confusing Euler (edges) and Hamilton (vertices).

activity.prompt: Read n, m and m undirected edges of a CONNECTED graph. Print CIRCUIT if an Euler circuit exists, PATH if only an Euler path exists, else NONE.
activity.hint: Count odd-degree vertices: 0, 2 or more.

quiz.q: Euler circuit requires all degrees to be
quiz.why: An Euler circuit uses each edge once and returns to the start. Each pass through a vertex uses one edge in and one out, so every degree must be even.
Every vertex of K_{3,3} has degree 3, which is odd. A graph with odd-degree vertices cannot have an Euler circuit.
K_{m,n} with m = n ≥ 2 is Hamiltonian, because a cycle can alternate between the two sides and visit every vertex. K_{3,3} has 3 + 3 vertices, so it works.
Dirac's condition (every degree ≥ n/2) guarantees a Hamiltonian cycle, so it is sufficient. It is not necessary: C₅ is Hamiltonian though every degree is 2 < 5/2.
The Petersen graph is the classic example of a graph that has no Hamiltonian cycle. It is not bipartite (it has 5-cycles) and has odd degrees, so it is not Eulerian.

scenes.text: An office has 5 computers. How many different tree-shaped networks connect them all?
Cayley's formula answers in one line: 5³ = 125.

steps.title: Tree facts
steps.body:
For a graph T on n vertices, these are equivalent: T is connected and acyclic; connected with n − 1 edges; acyclic with n − 1 edges; exactly one path between any two vertices.
- Every tree with n ≥ 2 has at least 2 leaves.
- A forest with c components has n − c edges.

steps.title: Solved example: leaves
steps.body:
A tree has 2 vertices of degree 4, 1 of degree 3, and the rest leaves. How many leaves?
- Let L leaves; n = 3 + L; edges = n − 1 = 2 + L.
- Degree sum: 8 + 3 + L = 2(2 + L) → 11 + L = 4 + 2L → **L = 7**.

steps.title: Counting spanning trees
steps.body:
- **Cayley**: Kₙ has n^(n−2) labelled spanning trees (via Prüfer codes of length n − 2).
- **Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem**: number of spanning trees = any cofactor of the Laplacian L = D − A.
- K_{m,n} has m^(n−1) n^(m−1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- n^(n−2) counts *labelled* trees, not shapes (unlabelled trees on 4 vertices: only 2).
- Forgetting that removing any edge of a tree disconnects it.
- Using n edges for a tree.

activity.prompt: Read n (2 ≤ n ≤ 15). Print the number of labelled spanning trees of Kₙ (Cayley's formula) as a long.
activity.hint: Multiply n by itself n−2 times.

quiz.q: Edges in a tree with 20 vertices
quiz.why: A tree on n vertices is connected and acyclic, with exactly n − 1 edges. For 20 vertices that is 19.
Cayley's formula gives nⁿ⁻² labelled spanning trees of Kₙ. For K₄ that is 4² = 16.

quiz.q: A forest with 12 vertices and 3 components has edges
quiz.why: A forest with n vertices and c components has n − c edges, since each tree has one fewer edge than vertices. Here 12 − 3 = 9.

quiz.q: Minimum leaves in a tree with ≥ 2 vertices
quiz.why: The two ends of a longest path cannot have other neighbours, or the path could be extended or a cycle would form. So both are leaves, giving at least 2.

quiz.q: Prüfer code length for a tree on n vertices
quiz.why: A Prüfer sequence has n − 2 entries, each from n labels. This gives a bijection with the n^(n−2) labelled trees.

scenes.text: A puzzle asks to connect three houses to water, gas and electricity without any lines crossing.
It is impossible: the graph is K_{3,3}, which is not planar.

steps.title: Planar graphs
steps.body:
Drawable without crossings. **Euler's formula** for connected planar graphs: **V − E + F = 2**.
- Simple, V ≥ 3: E ≤ 3V − 6. Triangle-free (e.g. bipartite): E ≤ 2V − 4.
- **Kuratowski**: planar iff no subdivision of K₅ or K_{3,3}.
- Every planar graph has a vertex of degree ≤ 5.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- K₅: E = 10 > 3·5 − 6 = 9 → **not planar**.
- K_{3,3}: E = 9 > 2·6 − 4 = 8 → **not planar**.
- A connected planar graph with 8 vertices and 12 edges has F = 2 − 8 + 12 = **6** faces (cube).

steps.title: Colouring
steps.body:
χ(G) = minimum colours so adjacent vertices differ.
- χ(Kₙ) = n; χ(Cₙ) = 2 (even) or 3 (odd); χ(tree) = 2; χ(bipartite) ≤ 2.
- **Four colour theorem**: planar ⇒ χ ≤ 4.
- Greedy colouring uses at most Δ + 1 colours; **Brooks**: χ ≤ Δ unless complete or odd cycle.

steps.title: Matchings
steps.body:
A matching is a set of disjoint edges; perfect if it covers every vertex.
- **Hall's theorem** (bipartite X, Y): a matching saturating X exists iff |N(S)| ≥ |S| for every S ⊆ X.
- **König**: in bipartite graphs, max matching = min vertex cover.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using E ≤ 3V − 6 to prove planarity (it is only necessary).
- Applying V − E + F = 2 to disconnected graphs (use V − E + F = 1 + c).
- Counting the outer face twice or forgetting it.

activity.prompt: Read V and E of a simple connected graph (V ≥ 3). Print FAILS if E > 3V − 6 (definitely not planar); otherwise print `faces=<F>` assuming it is planar (F = 2 − V + E).
activity.hint: K₄ is planar with 4 faces.

quiz.why: For a connected planar graph, V − E + F = 2, where F counts the outer face. The other forms give wrong values, for example for a single triangle.
K₄ can be drawn with one vertex inside the triangle formed by the other three, joined to each corner, with no crossings. So it is planar.

quiz.q: Maximum edges of a simple planar graph with 10 vertices
quiz.why: A simple planar graph with V ≥ 3 has E ≤ 3V − 6. For V = 10 this gives 30 − 6 = 24.
An odd cycle is not bipartite, so it needs at least 3 colours. Three colours are enough for any cycle, so χ(C₇) = 3.
Hall's condition says every set S of one side has at least |S| neighbours. It decides when a bipartite graph has a matching covering that side (the marriage theorem).

questions.q: Degree sum of a graph with 15 edges
questions.why: By the handshake lemma, the sum of degrees is 2E. With 15 edges it is 30.

questions.q: Is (4, 4, 4, 4, 4) graphical?
questions.why: Five vertices each of degree 4 means each is joined to every other vertex. That is exactly K₅, so the sequence is graphical.

questions.q: Is (5, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1) graphical?
questions.why: The degree sum 20 is even, but that alone is not enough. Havel–Hakimi: remove 5 and subtract 1 from the next five degrees, and the process eventually forces a negative degree, so the sequence is not graphical.

questions.q: Vertices in Q₄
questions.why: Qₙ has one vertex per n-bit string, so 2ⁿ vertices. For Q₄ that is 2⁴ = 16.

questions.q: Connected graph with degrees 2, 2, 3, 3, 4. Euler?
questions.why: A connected graph has an Euler path exactly when 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree, and a circuit only with 0. Degrees 3 and 3 are odd, so there is a path but no circuit.

questions.q: Assertion: K_{2,3} is not Hamiltonian. Reason: a Hamiltonian bipartite graph needs equal part sizes.
questions.why: K_{2,3} has parts of different sizes. A Hamiltonian cycle alternates sides, so it needs equal sizes, and the reason therefore explains the assertion.

questions.q: Tree with 4 vertices of degree 3 and the rest leaves. Leaves
questions.why: Degree sum = 2(edges) = 2(V − 1). With V = 4 + L, we get 12 + L = 2(3 + L), so L = 6.

questions.q: Spanning trees of K_{2,3}
